issues.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
issues.body:
A Daytona connection reset while a task machine runs a model command or the grader ends the rollout, and the quick loop masks it from training. In a Quick RL Loop run on 164 Linux and shell-simulator forge tasks (3 updates, 512 rollouts each), resets caused 2 of the 7 masked rollouts:

```
Task d13.stormwater.flood_risk/23 interrupted during advance: TaskMachineError (DaytonaConnectionError: Failed to execute command: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer)
Task d09.traffic_operations_control/17 interrupted during grade: TaskMachineError (DaytonaConnectionError: Failed to execute command: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer)
```

#11762 restarts a non-Harbor rollout only when the reset happens at `RolloutOperation.START`, before the model has run. A reset during `ADVANCE` or `GRADE` loses the turns already generated.

A third rollout in the same run failed with no cause in the log:

```
Task d40.animation.three_d.deforming_character_rig/14 interrupted during advance: TaskMachineError
```

`_failed_rollout` in `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_worker.py` appends the cause only when it is a `DaytonaError`, so any other cause of a `TaskMachineError` is not logged.

Done when:
- A connection reset during a command or during grading no longer discards the rollout when the command can be safely re-run or the rollout continued on a new machine.
- Every `TaskMachineError` warning names its underlying cause, redacted.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

One `Machine.run` on Daytona sends several provider requests: create the command directory, upload the script, run the script, measure and download the output, and remove the files ([`DaytonaMachine.run`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f6484db037/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L348-L465)). A `DaytonaConnectionError` from any of them leaves `run` unhandled. `_OwnedMachine.run` wraps it in a `TaskMachineError` ([machines.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f6484db037/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/machines.py#L40-L45)), and the task worker masks the rollout.

All of these requests except the one that runs the script give the same result when they run twice. The request that runs the script is different: the provider can start the command before the connection drops.

The warning has no cause for the third rollout because `_failed_rollout` appends the cause only when it is a `DaytonaError` ([task_worker.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f6484db037/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_worker.py#L323-L327)).

## Proposed Fix

1. The Daytona machine repeats a repeatable request that lost its connection, up to three times with backoff. `upload` and `download` restart as a whole.
2. The command script claims its private directory before it runs, and the exit trap records the exit code. After a lost connection the machine repeats the request, which starts the command only if the first request did not. The machine then reads the exit code from the sandbox until the command's timeout. The rollout keeps its turns and its machine.
3. `_failed_rollout` names the redacted cause of every `TaskMachineError`.

A connection that stays lost still masks the rollout. This change does not restart a rollout on a new machine after the model has run; #11762 does that only for a reset at machine start.

issues.author: malteosbot
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Not started. The plan trains the grug-MoE ladder (four model sizes, hidden width 512 to 1280) on two raw web-text corpora, each alone, with identical token budgets per rung. One corpus is US federal web pages from the End of Term 2024 archive. The other is a random sample of the six Common Crawl snapshots those pages were taken from. The comparison reports the loss on the Paloma eval suite and the choice loss on seven MMLU government subjects.

## Description

The [End of Term Web Archive](https://eotarchive.org/data/data-2024/) (EOT) collected US federal websites from September 2024 to April 2025. Its segment `CC-000` is Common Crawl's contribution: the federal captures of six Common Crawl snapshots, `CC-MAIN-2024-42`, `2024-46`, `2024-51`, `2025-05`, `2025-08` and `2025-13`, repackaged into new files. The segment includes Common Crawl's WET files, which hold the plain text that Common Crawl extracted from each page. There are 1,529 WET files, about 128 GB compressed (estimated from the sizes of 120 files), listed in `https://eotarchive.s3.amazonaws.com/crawl-data/EOT-2024/wet.paths.gz` under `segments/CC-000/wet/`. Each file belongs to one group: `GOV` (1,255 files), `MIL` (184) or `OTHER` (90, federal sites outside .gov and .mil, such as si.edu).

#6113 proposed this kind of comparison for Common Crawl's science Focus Crawl, and #6570 ran it at d512 and d768. There the main crawl had the lower Paloma macro loss (4.402 against 4.712 at d512), and the Focus Crawl had the lower loss on arXiv and S2ORC. #6570 reported no d1024 or d1280 result and did not measure MMLU. This experiment applies the same design to government text and adds a subject-specific eval.

### Arms

- `eot`: the `GOV` and `MIL` files of `CC-000` (1,439 files).
- `main`: a random sample of WET files from the same six `CC-MAIN` snapshots, read from `data.commoncrawl.org`. The sample takes files from each snapshot in the same proportion as the files sampled for the `eot` arm, counted from the path list.

Both arms use WET text with no further extraction or cleaning, except that exact duplicates (documents with identical text) are removed within each arm. `CC-000` holds up to six captures of the same pages, so the duplicate rate of the `eot` arm is reported. Files are sampled once, with sampling seed 0, and tokenized with the llama3 tokenizer, as in #6570.

Licensing: the EOT-2024 page says "There are no restrictions on the use, access, and/or download of data from the End of Term Web Archive Dataset", and asks users to cite the project. Works of the US government are in the public domain under 17 U.S.C. § 105. The `OTHER` group is left out because it includes bodies such as the Smithsonian, whose works are not US government works. Pages on .gov and .mil sites can still contain contractor or third-party content.

### Method

1. Ingest. Port #6570's WET reader (`lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/common_crawl_wet.py` on the unmerged branch `agent/grug-moe-crawl-compare`, last commit 2026-06-23) to the current default branch. For the `eot` arm, set its `base_url` to `https://eotarchive.s3.amazonaws.com` and read the paths from EOT's `wet.paths.gz`.
2. Pilot. Ingest and tokenize 20 files per arm. Measure tokens per file and the duplicate rate. Also report the share of documents that open with the banner "An official website of the United States government", as a measure of boilerplate in the `eot` arm. Then set the file counts so that each arm holds at least 1.24e10 tokens after duplicate removal. That is the d1280 budget; every rung draws from the same token pool of its arm, as in #6570, so the pool has to cover only the largest rung. An unmeasured estimate puts all of `CC-000` near 70B tokens before duplicate removal. If the `eot` arm holds fewer than 1.24e10 tokens, the top rung is the largest one whose budget the arm covers without repeating data.
3. Train. Train the grug-MoE compute-optimal ladder (`experiments/grug/moe`) on each arm alone, with #6570's rungs and token budgets. A rung is one model size, named by its hidden width (d512 has width 512), trained at the compute budget in the table. The model, optimizer, batch size and steps are the same for both arms at each rung. Each rung runs training seed 0, and d512 also runs training seeds 1 and 2 to measure the spread between seeds. The training seed sets the model initialization and the data order. The sampled files stay the same.

   | Rung | Compute budget (FLOPs) | Tokens | Reference runtime |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | d512 | 2.19e17 | 8.37e8 | 0.6 h |
   | d768 | 1.70e18 | 2.71e9 | 2.8 h |
   | d1024 | 9.00e18 | 6.63e9 | 10.5 h |
   | d1280 | 2.83e19 | 1.24e10 | 26.8 h |

   The runtimes are those of the reference runs in `experiments/grug/moe/README.md`, on one TPU v5p-8, and are a guide to cost only. Both arms train with the code of the current default branch, so their losses are not comparable with the numbers in #6570.
4. Keep ingestion, tokenization, training and checkpoints in one region. The d768 and larger runs of #6570 failed with `TransferBudgetExceeded`, the error Marin's storage layer raises when a job moves too much data between regions, until all steps ran in the same region.

### Metrics

- `eval/paloma/macro_loss` and the Paloma loss per source, at the end of each run.
- Choice loss on seven MMLU subjects, 1,081 questions in total: high_school_government_and_politics (193), us_foreign_policy (100), security_studies (245), jurisprudence (108), international_law (121), public_relations (110) and high_school_us_history (204). Choice loss is `−log2 softmax(ll)[gold]`, where `ll` holds the summed log-likelihood of each answer option, averaged over questions. `experiments/data_belay/accuracy.py` computes it, and its prompt format is used unchanged. Models of this size score near chance on multiple-choice accuracy, so accuracy is reported only as a check.
- Contamination: search both arms for the verbatim text of the questions in these seven subjects, and report the matches.

## Hypothesis or Goal

- H1: the `eot` arm has the lower choice loss on the seven MMLU government subjects.
- H2: the `main` arm has the lower Paloma macro loss, as the main crawl did against the Focus Crawl in #6570.

A difference between the arms counts as a result when it has the same sign at every rung and is larger than twice the standard deviation of that metric across the three d512 seeds, taking the larger of the two arms' standard deviations. Only d512 has more than one seed, so its spread is applied at every rung. That is an assumption.

If H1 holds, the next steps are to register `CC-000` in Datakit, Marin's registry of training data sources, and to ingest EOT-2024's larger segments, such as the Internet Archive's (699,060 WET files) and the Harvard Library Innovation Lab's (311,604). If H1 does not hold, EOT text adds nothing measurable over a general crawl on these subjects, and the larger segments are not ingested. H2 measures what the government text costs on general web text.

## Status

Not started. The cluster and accelerator are not chosen yet.

## Links

* EOT-2024 dataset page: https://eotarchive.org/data/data-2024/
* Prior work: #6113, #6570
* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-21: The `main` arm samples the six snapshots that `CC-000` was built from. Reusing #6570's `CC-MAIN-2024-18` arm (April 2024) would add crawl date as a second difference between the arms.
- 2026-11-21: The `OTHER` group is left out of the `eot` arm, for the licensing reason above.
- 2026-11-21: Exact duplicates are removed within each arm, because `CC-000` repeats pages across six snapshots.
- 2026-11-21: MMLU is scored with choice loss, because accuracy is near chance at these model sizes.

## Conclusion

None yet.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
Building any Micro210 step on main fails before GPU allocation, so Micro210 cannot score any model:

```
File "lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py", line 844, in _validate_skyrl_recipe
ValueError: SkyRL entrypoint is derived from the selected plan
```

The frozen Micro210 policy (`open-athena/micro210-policy@2026.11.20-together`) declares `entrypoint: generate` in its SkyRL config. #10737 added a check that rejects any declared `entrypoint`. `micro210_step` passes a `SkyRLRolePlan`. Dropping the `entrypoint` key and passing `SkyRLGenerationPlan` instead only moves the failure: `trainer.placement.colocate_all=True disagrees with the role plan value False`. So the frozen protocol and SkyRL's plan validation disagree on more than the entrypoint.

Reproduce:
1. On main, with CoreWeave S3 credentials exported, run:
   `uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.micro210 --model-uri s3://marin-us-east-08a/tmp/x --model-manifest-sha256 <64 zeros> --tokenizer-uri meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --tokenizer-revision <40 zeros> --name evaluation/micro210/repro --version 2026.11.20.1`
2. The command fails with the error above while planning.

Expected: Micro210 plans a generation-only evaluation from the frozen policy. Either the policy config maps onto a SkyRL plan that validation accepts, or the policy is re-pinned under a new version without the conflicting keys.

This blocks #11902 (Micro210 after RL, part of #11862).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 PR [#11919](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11919) already addresses this failure and includes `Fixes #11916`. It builds a `SkyRLGenerationPlan` from the frozen policy's inference geometry, removes the declared `entrypoint` and `colocate_all` values before plan validation, and adds a launch assertion for `entrypoint: generate`. CI is still running; this issue is handed off to that PR.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
`find_free_port(start=10000)` writes a per-port lock file containing the caller's PID under a shared temp directory and treats any port whose lock-file PID is alive (`os.kill(pid, 0)`) as taken, even when nothing is bound to it. Neither the Kubernetes port-forward context nor the GCP SSH tunnel context removes the lock file when the tunnel closes, so a long-lived polling process leaks one port lock on every client open. Once 1,000 locks accumulate across live processes, every Iris client and CLI call on the host fails with `No free port found in range 10000-11000`, blocking other users on the same host.

Reproduce:
1. In a long-lived process, repeatedly open and close an Iris client using a Kubernetes port-forward (`k8s/service.py`) or GCP SSH tunnel (`gcp/controller.py`).
2. Observe each open writing a new per-port lock file (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/types.py:85, 95`) that remains on disk after the tunnel exits and the port is unbound.
3. Once 1,000 locks exist across live PIDs, open any Iris client or run an Iris CLI command on the host; it fails with `Could not connect to controller: No free port found in range 10000-11000`.

Expected: Release the port lock file when the client or tunnel context exits (including startup failure paths), or reuse one tunnel/port per process, and avoid treating an unbound port as permanently locked for the caller's lifetime.

## Where (verified on `main` `e4cf2e6fa2`)

- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/types.py:72-99`: `find_free_port` scans `range(start, start + 1000)` (`L84`), skips any port whose lock file (`L85`) holds a live PID (`os.kill(int(lock.read_text()), 0)` at `L87-88`), writes `str(os.getpid())` (`L95`), and raises `RuntimeError(f"No free port found in range {start}-{start + 1000}")` (`L99`). No unlock/unlink helper exists, and nothing else in `lib/iris/src` removes these lock files.
- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/service.py:816-817, 917-922`: `port_forward` calls `find_free_port(start=10000)` and stops `kubectl port-forward` in `finally:` without removing the lock file.
- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/gcp/controller.py:280-281, 308-317`: the GCP SSH tunnel context calls `find_free_port(start=10000)` and terminates the SSH process in `finally:` without removing the lock file.

## Observed evidence (`2026-11-21 00:00:13Z–00:03:00Z`)

- Every `open_iris_client` call against regional CoreWeave configs (`cw-us-east-02a`, `cw-rno2a`) across 7 long-lived polling processes on a shared host failed with `ClickException Could not connect to controller: No free port found in range 10000-11000`; other CLI calls on the same host also failed.
- At `00:02Z`, all 1,000 lock files were present while `ss -ltn` showed only 2 active listeners in `10000–11000`. **993 of 1,000** unbound locks were held by live polling processes (held across 7 polling PIDs: `211`, `208`, `208`, `191`, `138`, `26`, and `11` locks, with the remaining 7 of 1,000 across the 2 listeners and single-lock PIDs; growing at ~30 locks/min across 7 pollers). Deleting the 993 unbound lock files immediately restored client connectivity.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`find_free_port(start=10000)` writes a PID lock for each chosen port. The [Kubernetes tunnel](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/service.py#L812) and [GCP tunnel](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/gcp/controller.py#L248) stop their subprocesses without releasing those locks, so repeated client opens in a live process exhaust the 1,000-port scan.

**Relevant code**
- [`types.py#L70`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/types.py#L70) — port selection and PID lock
- [`service.py#L812`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/service.py#L812) — Kubernetes port-forward lifecycle
- [`controller.py#L248`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/gcp/controller.py#L248) — GCP SSH tunnel lifecycle

# Proposed Fix

Both tunnel contexts call `find_free_port` before starting their subprocesses, but their cleanup only stops the subprocess. Add a scoped port reservation that releases its lock on normal exit and startup failure, and use it in both tunnel contexts.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Snowball (67B-A2B) serving on TPU v4 with TP=8 fails during precompile: the MoE grouped-matmul kernel needs more VMEM than a v4 core has. This blocks the smallest slice that fits the weights (v4-16, 8 chips). Part of https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11855.

## Repro

- Model: `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05` @ `ac60d940`.
- Stack: marin PR 11780 plus PR 11781's tpu-inference pin `03f10d39` (vLLM `fb02daf1`).
- Command: `marin-serve iris <model> --cluster marin --tpu v4-16 --region us-central2 --no-preemptible --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 32768 --memory 300g --wait-timeout 3600`. `--no-preemptible` is added in the task/535 draft PR.
- Result: weights load. Then `_precompile_backbone_text_only` fails with:

```
RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: XLA:TPU compile permanent error. Ran out of memory in memory space vmem.
Used 16.22M of 16.00M vmem. Exceeded vmem capacity by 224.0K.
XLA label: gmm_v2-g_256-m_512-k_2560-act_silu-n_512-tm_512-tk_2560-tn_256
```

## Cause

`tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py`:
- `gmm` sets `vmem_limit_bytes` to 90% of VMEM capacity.
- `calculate_tiling` then grows `tile_m` in up to 4 buckets while `_gmm_vmem_estimate` stays under that limit.
- For these shapes, the estimate is about 14.7 MB (LHS 5.2 + RHS 7.9 + accumulator 1.0 + output 0.5). The compiled kernel uses 16.22 MB.
- The estimate leaves out the other scratch buffers, such as the zero-fill tile and the per-sublane output buffer, plus compiler scratch.
- A v4 core has 16 MiB of VMEM, so the gap overflows it. v5p and v6e have much larger VMEM, so they don't hit it.
- `tile_m` reaches 512 for any batch of 512 or more rows, so no serving flag avoids it.
- Upstream tpu-inference has since removed this local `gmm_v2` copy (commit `9dc239779`, "Remove the local copy of gmm v2"). That landed after our fork base `34535b11`.

## Options

1. **Serve on v4-32 with TP=16** (no code change). Each device then holds half of the expert matmul, so the same tiles need about 10–12 MB. This is the route that served Snowball on v4 in October. It is being tested now.
2. **Patch the fork's `calculate_tiling`** so v4-16 works. For example, count the missing scratch buffers in `_gmm_vmem_estimate`, or keep more headroom when VMEM is 16 MiB or less. This needs a fork PR, a Marin re-pin and the TPU release gate. A rebase onto upstream's tokamax kernel may also fix it; that is not checked.

## Decision needed

Whether v4-16 (8 chips) is worth option 2, or whether v4-32 (16 chips) is fine for the shared endpoint.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The fork's `calculate_tiling` budgets LHS, RHS, accumulator, and output tiles, but `gmm_v2` also declares VMEM scratch for partial output and zero fill. The 90% budget therefore admits the reported `tile_m=512` shape even though compilation exceeds the v4 core's 16 MiB VMEM. [tpu-inference #36](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/pull/36) fixes chip allocation, and [Marin #11781](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11781) pins that fix; neither changes this kernel. No result for the proposed v4-32/TP=16 run is posted here or in [#11855](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11855).

**Relevant code**

- [`gmm_v2.py#L962-L1041`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/03f10d39fd1786fdcd5cab1d1c98bc01c2b5155a/tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py#L962-L1041) — VMEM estimate and tile growth.
- [`gmm_v2.py#L1337-L1377`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/03f10d39fd1786fdcd5cab1d1c98bc01c2b5155a/tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py#L1337-L1377) — additional VMEM scratch.
- [`gmm_v2.py#L1307-L1308`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/03f10d39fd1786fdcd5cab1d1c98bc01c2b5155a/tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py#L1307-L1308) — 90% default budget.

# Proposed Fix

1. Complete the v4-32/TP=16 run with model revision `ac60d940`, the same backend pin and 32K context. Record the job, precompile outcome, a successful request, KV capacity, and latency. This establishes whether the 16-chip endpoint is usable.
2. If that run meets the endpoint's needs and its 16-chip footprint is acceptable, record the decision and close this issue as a v4-16 limitation.
3. If v4-16 is required, reproduce the failing shape in the tpu-inference fork and change tiling to account for the omitted scratch or reserve enough measured headroom. Add a regression for the selected v4 tile, verify full precompile and requests on v4-16, run the TPU release gate, then re-pin Marin in a PR with `Fixes #11920`.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

`lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_guard.py` (`install_gpu_compile_guard` -> `guarded_compile_or_get_cached`) currently verifies that all participating GPU ranks agree on the **pre-compile** JAX cache key before invoking XLA compilation, but does not check whether the **post-compile** executable matches across ranks before execution begins.

Recent evidence on issue 11793 (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793) shows that 64 ranks with an identical pre-compile `cache_key` can still compile different optimized HLO executables (because `--xla_gpu_per_fusion_autotune_cache_dir` is excluded from JAX's compilation cache key, and `executable_fingerprint` alone does not always change when compiled HLO text changes). When two variants schedule independent global collectives in opposite blocking order under `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=1`, the job can stall silently on step 0 instead of failing with an error.

Adding a post-compile `executable_text_sha256` equality check in `compile_guard.py` turns any cross-rank executable divergence (from autotune inputs, flags, environment, or future regressions) from a silent multi-node hang into an immediate, actionable error before step 0 enters NCCL.

## Where this should live (verified on `main` `eccbd0f8c5`)

- **Implementation:** `lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_guard.py`, inside `install_gpu_compile_guard()` -> `guarded_compile_or_get_cached()` (immediately after `original(...)` returns `xc.LoadedExecutable`, lines 133–135).
  - `initialize_jax()` in `lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py` already installs this guard for multi-process GPU jobs (lines 315 and 365), so placing the check here covers every multi-process GPU trainer (Levanter, Grug, SFT, custom workers) in one spot.
- **Unit tests:** `lib/iris/tests/test_jax_compile_guard.py`.

## Proposed behavior

1. **Compute compiled HLO text SHA-256 on each participating rank** right after `loaded = original(...)` returns for `backend.platform == "gpu" and len(process_ids) > 1`:
   - Extract the optimized HLO text from `loaded` using the same fallback chain as JAX's `MeshExecutable.as_text()`:
     - `loaded.get_hlo_text()` if present, else `"\n\n".join(m.to_string() for m in loaded.hlo_modules())`.
     - If unavailable (`NotImplementedError` or `JaxRuntimeError` starting with `UNIMPLEMENTED`), log a warning once and return `loaded` without breaking unsupported backends.
   - Hash the UTF-8 encoded text with `hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest()`.
2. **Collect per-rank autotune folder metadata** (best-effort, non-fatal):
   - Parse `--xla_gpu_per_fusion_autotune_cache_dir=...` from `os.environ.get("XLA_FLAGS", "")` (or empty string if unset/empty).
   - Count files in that directory if it exists (or `0` if empty/missing).
3. **Second CPU-only rendezvous over the existing JAX distributed KV store** (reusing `_CompileGuardState` and `_Coordinator`: `key_value_set`, `wait_at_barrier`, `key_value_dir_get`, `key_value_delete` under a **separate** key prefix and sequence counter, e.g. `iris/compile-executable-hash/v1/{group}/{sequence}/`, run after `original(...)` returns):
   - Never use GPU collectives (`sync_global_devices`) for this check, since the whole purpose is to catch divergence before any GPU collective runs.
   - **Timeout sizing for compile-time skew:** The post-compile barrier timeout must cover cross-rank compile-time skew (observed `12–25 s` cold compile spread in issue 11793, and potentially minutes on larger programs), not only the KV exchange itself — reuse `_COMPILE_FINGERPRINT_TIMEOUT_MS` (`30 min`, `compile_guard.py:20`) or a dedicated timeout sized at least as large as `_COMPILE_FINGERPRINT_TIMEOUT_MS`, and on timeout raise `RuntimeError` with the observed per-rank map just like the pre-compile check (`compile_guard.py:49-54`).
   - Each rank publishes a small JSON record `{"text_sha256": ..., "autotune_dir": ..., "autotune_file_count": ...}`.
4. **Fail fast on mismatch:**
   - If `set(observed) != set(process_ids)` or `len(distinct_text_hashes) != 1`, raise `RuntimeError` immediately before returning the compiled executable.
   - Include in the error message:
     - the pre-compile `cache_key` (fingerprint that matched across ranks),
     - the count of distinct `executable_text_sha256` values,
     - each distinct `executable_text_sha256` mapped to its sorted list of `process_id`s,
     - each rank's active autotune directory and file count (compact summary grouped by hash or per rank).
5. **Behavior on persistent cache hits:** On a persistent compilation-cache hit, every rank deserializes process 0's executable, so the post-compile hash check passes trivially. That is the intended behavior, and should be noted so a pass on a cache hit is not misread as proof that per-rank compile inputs were uniform.

## Overhead

- `as_text()` / `hlo_modules()` plus `sha256` runs on every multi-process GPU compile (`~3–7 MB` of HLO text for `jit_train_step`, well under 1 second, plus ~150 bytes/rank over CPU gRPC once per compilation, not per training step). Small JITs pay this cost as well, so the implementation should either keep it always-on after measuring small-JIT overhead or gate it on executables above a size threshold.

## Acceptance criteria

- Existing unit tests in `lib/iris/tests/test_jax_compile_guard.py` continue to pass.
- New unit tests verify:
  1. Identical post-compile HLO text hashes across ranks pass cleanly and clean up KV keys.
  2. Mismatched post-compile HLO text hashes under an identical pre-compile cache key raise `RuntimeError` containing the distinct hash count, per-hash rank lists, and per-rank autotune folder file counts.
  3. Backends whose executable does not implement `get_hlo_text` / `hlo_modules` log a warning and do not crash.
- Related issues:
  - https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793
  - https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11909
  - https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11775

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The existing guard compares JAX cache keys before compilation, then returns the loaded executable without comparing optimized HLO. Issue #11793 records 64 ranks with one cache key and three distinct executable text hashes; two variants schedule global collectives in opposite order. No open PR references #11917.

**Relevant code**
- [`compile_guard.py#L34-L86`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_guard.py#L34-L86) — existing CPU coordinator exchange and sequence state.
- [`compile_guard.py#L107-L135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_guard.py#L107-L135) — shared JAX compile entry point.
- [`test_jax_compile_guard.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/iris/tests/test_jax_compile_guard.py) — in-memory coordinator tests.

# Proposed Fix

After `compile_or_get_cached` returns on multi-process GPU jobs, hash the optimized HLO text and exchange each rank's hash and autotune-directory metadata through a second, separately keyed CPU coordinator rendezvous. Raise before executable return if hashes differ, with the cache key, grouped rank hashes, and per-rank autotune file counts; keep the 30-minute timeout for compile skew. Publish an unsupported-text status through the same rendezvous so one rank cannot skip while peers wait, then warn and continue if any rank lacks the text API. Add two-rank regression tests for matching, mismatched, and unsupported text, including key cleanup.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 Fixed in [PR #11923](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11923). The guard now compares optimized HLO text across ranks after compilation and raises with grouped hashes and autotune metadata before executable return. The Iris safe suite passed (3,102 tests); the final focused guard run passed 11 tests, and the changed module has zero Pyrefly errors. Production GPU overhead remains unmeasured.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Six BixBench trials in Mochi base Micro210 `2026.11.20.7` failed with `ValueError: Environment variable 'OPENAI_API_KEY' not found in host environment`, despite a configured remote judge. Four other BixBench trials failed during setup and never reached verification.

Reproduce:
1. Use runtime `ea21a69e55` with the `2026.11.20-together` policy and an original Harbor BixBench trial.
2. Pass the remote judge through `environment.task_sessions.remote_judge`, with its credential delivered on the host.
3. Run verification; it raises the missing `OPENAI_API_KEY` error.

Expected: verifier calls use the host-authenticated judge relay. Guests receive a localhost endpoint and dummy credential; the provider key stays on the host.

`InstalledAgentRuntime` passes `guest_environment={}` to `Trial.create` and does not bind verifier declarations to `lowered.judge_connection`. Harbor resolves credential templates against this captured guest environment. Proposed fix: adapt the binding helper from #11787 without restoring `installed_agent.judge_model`.

The root run is `/benfeuer/mochi-base-micro210-eval-2026.11.20.7-coordinator-f1c15483`. [Failure audit in Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fmochi-long-loop%2Fmochi-base-micro210-eval%2F2026.11.20.7%2Freport%2Ffailure-audit.json): `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/mochi-long-loop/mochi-base-micro210-eval/2026.11.20.7/report/failure-audit.json`. The audit records the policy SHA and traceback evidence.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`TaskRolloutWorker._generate()` attaches `judge_connection` after constructing the original Harbor harness, so the harness captures a task without the connection. `InstalledAgentRuntime` then passes no model authentication and an empty guest environment to `Trial.create`; Harbor cannot resolve the verifier's `${OPENAI_API_KEY}` template.

**Relevant code**
- [`task_worker.py#L491-L497`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_worker.py#L491-L497) — connection attached after harness construction
- [`agent_runtime.py#L210-L236`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L210-L236) — bindings applied, trial receives empty environment
- [`verifier.py#L206-L225`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/verifier/verifier.py#L206-L225) — verifier resolves declared variables
- [`host_capabilities.py#L91-L126`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/host_capabilities.py#L91-L126) — existing guest relay projection

# Proposed Fix

Attach `judge_connection` before selecting the harness. After restoring `task.toml` and applying task bindings, derive the declared judge model, bind `lowered.judge_connection` to the trial's host model authentication, and rewrite verifier variables with `model_guest_environment`. Pass runtime relay variables only when the task environment declares model access; verify templated and literal verifier endpoints through Harbor's `Verifier.verify`, with the host key absent from guest commands.

[PR #11787](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11787) already implements verifier routing in this runtime, but adds `installed_agent.judge_model`; reconcile its open changes with the connection-based path above before landing this fix. No parallel PR opened against the same runtime.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Summary

`fetch_file_set()` in `lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py` unconditionally rewrites every file in a FineStore bucket via `atomic_rename()` on every job start, while `FineStoreDirectory` uploads every pre-existing leftover file from persistent `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/process-0` into the current `tree_hash`'s FineStore bucket. Because `configure_jax_compilation_cache()` runs synchronously before `jax.distributed.initialize()` with no timeout, size cap, or progress logging, multi-million-file stores add `6.5–7 minutes` of startup overhead on healthy nodes and caused 3 separate 64-GPU jobs to fail before compilation on a node with slower small-file XFS writes.

*(This issue tracks the contained fetch/upload fixes; the broader multi-rank autotune uniformity redesign is tracked separately.)*

## Confirmed defects on `main` (`7210b12a88`)

1. **Unconditional full rewrite on every start (`lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py:34-53`):**
   - `fetch_file_set(root, local)` iterates every descriptor in `BlobTables.DESCRIPTORS` and unconditionally stages and renames each file (`atomic_rename()` at `:48` -> `Path.open("wb")` at `:49`), even when `target` already exists on `/cache` with the same size (`BlobDescriptor` already carries `name` and `size` at `lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py:200-215`).
2. **Pre-existing host leftovers uploaded into FineStore (`lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py:95-100, 111-116`, `lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py:76, 92-93`):**
   - `compile_cache.py` points global rank 0 (`UPLOADER`) at persistent uncleaned `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune/process-0` (`makedirs(exist_ok=True)`).
   - `FineStoreDirectory.__init__` sets `self._known = fetch_file_set(self._root, local)` (`:76`), and `flush()` uploads `pending = sorted(present - self._known)` (`:92-93`) — pushing every pre-existing local leftover into the current `tree_hash` bucket.
   - Observed remote store sizes: **`2,786,218` logical files** (`168` objects, `246.98 MiB` compressed in object storage) in one `tree_hash` bucket and **`2,786,196` logical files** (`417` objects, `517.47 MiB` compressed) in another — expanding to **`~11 GiB`** on local disk per node at 4 KiB block granularity.
3. **Unbounded, silent pre-init fetch (`lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py:279`, `compile_cache.py:116`, `fileset.py:34-53`):**
   - `configure_jax_compilation_cache()` runs before `jax.distributed.initialize()` with no timeout, no file-count or byte cap, and no progress logging after `XLA per-fusion autotune cache: <dir>`.

## Observed impact (3 failed 64-GPU jobs in one night)

- **Healthy nodes:** Rewriting `2.79M` files (`~11 GiB`) per fetcher rank (`process_index % 8 == 0`) runs at ~`7,000 files/s` and takes **`6.5–7 minutes`** before distributed init (`~6 min 38 s` observed across `2,786,218–2,786,492` files / `~11 GiB` per node).
- **Slow-disk node:** On one node whose local `/cache` XFS array writes small files ~10x slower (~`650 files/s`; measured `240,961 -> 265,697` rewritten files in `38 s`, projecting to ~`70 min` for `2.79M` files, with kernel D-state samples in `rename()` / `wchan __flush_work` and `Path.open` / `wchan xfs_buf_lock`), 3 separate 64-GPU jobs failed before compiling:
  1. **Pre-job:** One fetcher rank (`process 8`) logged nothing for `36 min 48 s` after `XLA per-fusion autotune cache:`, until all 63 peer ranks failed on `CoordinationService/RegisterTask` (`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, 30-min deadline).
  2. **Training run:** `process 8` spent `>20 min` inside `fetch_file_set` -> `atomic_rename` (`rename()` / `__flush_work`, `2,786,318` files / `~11 GiB`) while 63 peers waited in JAX init; cancelled before reaching training.
  3. **Diagnostic run:** `process 8` rewrote at ~`650 files/s` (`~265k / 2.79M` in `7.5 min`, ~`70 min` projected vs. the 30-min `RegisterTask` deadline); cancelled before reaching training.

## Expected / requested fixes

1. **Skip-if-present in `fetch_file_set()` (`fileset.py:34-53`):** Before staging and `atomic_rename()`, check whether `target` already exists locally with matching `descriptor.size` (and/or digest/metadata), avoiding millions of redundant small-file writes on warm `/cache` volumes.
2. **Bound and instrument the fetch (`compile_cache.py:116`, `fileset.py:34-53`):** Add a configurable timeout, a max file-count / byte cap, and periodic progress logging (elapsed time, files written/skipped, files/s) so a slow node or bloated store fails fast and visibly instead of hanging silently until `RegisterTask` expires (and raise rather than silently falling back to an inconsistent partial folder).
3. **Stop uploading pre-existing leftovers (`fileset.py:76, 92-93`, `compile_cache.py:113-114`):** Seed `FineStoreDirectory._known` with all files already present in `local` at `__init__` (not only the fetched set) so `flush()` uploads only files newly created during the current run, and skip starting the uploader thread when `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`.

## Acceptance criteria

- Unit tests in `lib/finestore/tests/test_fileset.py` and `lib/iris/tests/` (e.g. `test_jax_init.py` or a new `test_jax_compile_cache.py`) verify:
  1. `fetch_file_set()` skips rewriting existing matching files (zero `atomic_rename` calls on a warm repeat fetch) while still writing missing or size-mismatched files.
  2. Fetch timeout, max file-count / byte cap, and periodic progress logs trigger cleanly and fail loudly on breach.
  3. `FineStoreDirectory` seeded against a directory with pre-existing leftover files uploads `0` pre-existing files on `flush()`, uploading only files created after `__init__`.
  4. `configure_jax_compilation_cache()` does not start the `FineStoreDirectory` uploader thread when `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`.

## Related issues

- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11909
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11775
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11917

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

## Research

[`fetch_file_set()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py#L34-L53) rewrites every descriptor, and [`FineStoreDirectory`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/finestore/src/finestore/fileset.py#L64-L93) only excludes fetched paths from later uploads. The node-local directory persists across builds, while [`configure_jax_compilation_cache()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py#L91-L116) fetches synchronously before distributed initialization. The existing [fetch wrapper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7210b12a8864daaace69a519267960576a8eb0f4/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/compile_cache.py#L138-L145) also treats an I/O failure after partial materialization as a cold start. I found no open PR for this path.

## Proposed Fix

This needs a bounded fetch contract across FineStore and Iris, with these implementation steps:

1. Give `fetch_file_set()` explicit file-count, logical-byte, deadline, and progress settings. Count every descriptor, including skipped files; check limits before writing, report elapsed time and written/skipped counts periodically, and raise a specific error on breach. Skip an existing regular file only when its recorded size matches. Namespace the local directory by `tree_hash` (or verify a stored digest) so a same-size file from another build cannot be mistaken for a match. A deadline checked between files cannot interrupt one blocked XFS operation; enforce the startup deadline outside the fetch worker if the timeout must cover blocked I/O.
2. Seed `FineStoreDirectory`'s known paths from the local directory after fetching and before starting its thread. Its first and later flushes should publish only files created after construction. Treat fetch-limit and timeout errors as startup failures, including when a partial directory remains; keep any separate policy for an object-store outage explicit.
3. In Iris, parse `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` before choosing an uploader or fetcher and avoid creating the synchronizer in that mode. Pass the fetch settings from one documented configuration point.
4. Add temp-directory FineStore regressions for warm reuse, missing and mismatched files, both caps, timeout, progress, and leftover exclusion. Add Iris coverage for level 0 and failure propagation. Then run affected safe tests, required formatting and lint review, and publish a PR with `Fixes #11925`.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The frozen Micro210 CRUXEval path scores correct answers 0.0 in ways the upstream
benchmark harness does not. On the standard89 A/B slice (10 CRUXEval-O tasks per arm,
sealed 2026-11-20), arm A scored 1/10 and arm B 0/10; replaying the frozen grader and
the upstream facebookresearch/cruxeval harness on the same graded text gives 6/10 and
5/10. Three independent defects:

1. `<|eot_id|>` in the graded answer text. The launch sets `skip_special_tokens:
   false`; the model client restores the turn terminator into assistant content, and
   `/app/answer.txt` therefore ends in `<|eot_id|>`. For answers without a closed
   `[ANSWER]…[/ANSWER]` pair, `eval/graders/programs.py::crux` leaves the token inside
   the extracted literal and the assertion fails to parse. Five arm-A attempts with
   correct literals were zeroed this way; all five pass once the token is removed.
2. `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` in
   `eval/chat_benchmarks/CruxEval/execution.py::check_correctness` (upstream uses the
   default fork context). Under spawn the child re-imports the grader's `__main__`
   (`/tests/grade.py` imports the evalchemy wheel, lm_eval, datasets, aiohttp) inside
   the parent's `join(timeout+1)` = 11 s window, so on a cold verifier machine any
   trial is recorded `timed out` → 0.0 with a normal exit. Four arm-B attempts
   (uids 54/36/45/27) carry clean closed-tag answers with correct literals that the
   frozen grader itself passes on every reconstructable payload, yet the sealed
   verifier returned 0.0. The same signature appears in the round-1 seal evidence
   (issue #11337; UIDs 44/88/132: verifier exit 0, stdout `0.0`). Mechanism
   demonstrated locally: a 12 s child-side `__main__` import yields
   `result='timed out', passed=False` for a trivially correct program; 3 s passes.
3. `re.search(r"f\(.*?\)", …)` in the crux grader (and the same regex in
   `lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/assets/code_protocol.py`)
   stops at the first `)`, which sits inside tuple arguments, so calls like
   `f([('u', 1), ('s', 7), ('u', -5)])` are only partially removed and the literal is
   destroyed. Upstream splits at `==` instead and is immune.

Not a defect: answers wrapped in code fences without `[ANSWER]` tags fail under the
upstream harness too (upstream strips whitespace but not fences); those zeros are
model behavior.

Reproduce:
1. Unzip the frozen wheel (`evalchemy-frozen.whl`, sha256 `9970bac6…657`) and read
   `eval/graders/programs.py::crux` and `eval/chat_benchmarks/CruxEval/execution.py`.
2. Replay `crux()` on the standard89 arm-A CRUXEval rows' final assistant messages,
   with and without a trailing `<|eot_id|>`: five correct-literal attempts flip from
   syntax-error-0 to pass without the token.
3. Replay `crux()` on arm-B uids 54/36/45/27 (clean `[ANSWER]` pairs, correct
   literals): the extraction passes all four while the sealed `verification.score`
   is 0.0.
4. Run the spawn demo: call the wheel's `check_correctness` from a `__main__` whose
   module imports take ≥ ~11 s (e.g. `time.sleep(12)` at module level); a trivially
   correct program returns `timed out`/`passed=False`.

Expected: CRUXEval verdicts reflect the answer's correctness under the upstream
protocol — graded text free of special tokens, call removal that handles nested
parentheses, and child-process startup that does not count against the execution
timeout.

Evidence: the standard89 A/B scoring packet `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/long-loop-exp4/evidence/eot-standard89-ab-scores/manifest.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Flong-loop-exp4%2Fevidence%2Feot-standard89-ab-scores%2Fmanifest.json)) and the slice-B trial receipts (verifier stdout and staged `answer.txt`) for uids 54/36/45/27. Related: #11337, #10828.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The shared grader scores a PASS from zero evidence when a task has no FAIL_TO_PASS and no PASS_TO_PASS ids and the parsed test log is empty.

`grade()` resolves a task when the parsed PASSED set is a subset of the expected set. With empty id lists the expected set is empty, so an empty parse is a vacuous subset and `resolved` is true. `test.sh` then writes reward 1. `test.sh` writes reward 0 when `resolved` is false.

Impact: the reward is noise. Two trials with identical empty evidence score differently. We saw this on one converted task row. Its grader scored 1.0 on the upstream image side and 0.0 on the repaired-base side from identical empty logs. The row cannot carry a meaningful fidelity verdict, so it is held out of admission.

Reproduce:
1. Build a task config with `"FAIL_TO_PASS": []` and `"PASS_TO_PASS": []`.
2. Run `grade(config, "")` on an empty log.
3. `grade()` returns `resolved: true`. `grade.py` exits 0. `test.sh` writes reward 1.
4. Run `grade(config, "PASSED tests/test_a.py::test_one\n")` on a log with one parsed test.
5. `grade()` returns `resolved: false` from the same empty id lists. `test.sh` writes reward 0.

Expected: a task with no test ids and an empty parsed log is UNSCORABLE. The grader must not resolve it. It must not score a pass. The verdict should say so in the log.

Fix (in review): `grade()` now marks the empty-ids-and-empty-log case as `unscorable`, forces `resolved` false, prints `UNSCORABLE`, and exits 1. `test.sh` then leaves reward 0. Tasks with test ids keep the old verdict logic. A behavior test covers the three cases.

Evidence:
- Repro row: `nvim-lua__plenary.nvim-251` (SWE-rebench V2.1 repair fidelity gate, sample manifest 200 rows).
- Upstream-image trial receipt: exit 0, `test_output.log` empty, elapsed 18 s, `verdict.json` = `{"detail": {"exit_code": 0}, "reward": 1.0, "status": "scored"}`.
- Repaired-base trial receipt: exit 0, `test_output.log` empty, `verdict.json` = `{"detail": {"exit_code": 0}, "reward": 0.0, "status": "scored"}` (the real run parsed tests, so the subset check failed).
- Row data: `FAIL_TO_PASS` is null. The grader had no ids to check on either side.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A symbolic math reply that is equal to the reference only under positivity assumptions scores 0, because math-verify's comparison cannot prove the identity for unassumed symbols. The grader never awards a false positive here — the failure mode is a conservative false negative on an equivalent answer. On the HARDMath mirror (`pafitis/HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10`), 89 of 89 symbolic-nondimensionalization rows whose reference carries a power of a ratio score 0 when the reply regroups the same expression into a ratio of powers (89 of the 101 `nondimensionalization_symbolic` rows have that form; measured through `verifyit.grade.run` under the `convert_hardmath_rhs` contracts, replay in [#11511 (comment)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11511#issuecomment-7006269885)). This is independent of the member-splitting bug fixed in #11739.

Reproduce:
1. Grade a regrouped reply against its reference with the symbolic math grader:

    ```python
    from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
    from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

    # HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10, question_type nondimensionalization_symbolic
    cases = [
        (r"\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{3}}",
         r"\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{19}{9}} a_{3}}"),  # row 9
        (r"\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{17}{6}}}{a_{3}}",
         r"\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{17}{6}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{17}{6}} a_{3}}"),  # row 20
        (r"\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{5}{4}}}{a_{3}}",
         r"\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{\frac{5}{4}}}{a_{2}^{\frac{5}{4}} a_{3}}"),    # row 29
    ]
    for reference, reply in cases:
        spec = MathSpec(expected=reference, math_type=MathType.SCALAR)
        print(grade_math_candidate(spec, reply).reward)  # 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    ```

2. Each row prints 0.0; the reference itself, the reply form with the outer ratio kept, and wrong replies grade normally, so the 0 comes from the comparison of two parsed expressions, not from a parse failure.

Expected: the regrouped reply grades 1.0. It equals the reference wherever the coefficients are positive, and these datasets' coefficients are positive constants (for example `1.00`); a silent 0 for a semantically correct answer shape undercounts measured solve rates for any source whose answers contain powers of ratios.

Confirmed root cause of the 0: both sides parse to expressions, and the equality needs positivity. Row 9 parses to `a_1*(a_3/a_2)**(19/9)/a_3` (reference) and `a_1*a_3**(19/9)/(a_2**(19/9)*a_3)` (reply); `sympy.simplify(gold - target)` without assumptions leaves a nonzero difference, and the same simplify with the symbols declared `positive=True` returns exactly 0.

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The reported regrouping parses on both sides, but `math_verify.verify` compares symbols without the positivity needed to prove the identity. VerifyIt has no domain assumptions in `MathSpec`; the shared task converter constructs that spec without source-specific symbol metadata. A global positive-symbol rule would change scores for tasks with unrestricted variables (for example, `\sqrt{x^2}` versus `x` at negative `x`).

**Relevant code**
- [`grade_math.py#L106-L155`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L106-L155) — symbolic comparison
- [`grade_math.py#L367-L405`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L367-L405) — candidate scoring
- [`spec.py#L143-L149`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/spec.py#L143-L149) — math contract fields
- [`answers.py#L108-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/convert/answers.py#L108-L123) — shared spec construction
- [`math.py#L209-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a8a628d2613b3b730f84ea317c99e8c5f2c94a8/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/math.py#L209-L215) — HARDMath conversion on main

# Proposed Fix

1. Audit the 89 affected `nondimensionalization_symbolic` questions in `pafitis/HARDMath_processed_training@937e9f10` for an explicit positive domain for each symbolic coefficient. The presence of positive numeric constants alone does not establish the domain of every symbol. Record any exceptions and leave those contracts unchanged.
2. Add an opt-in tuple of positive symbol names to `MathSpec`, defaulting to empty. After ordinary scalar comparison fails, substitute positive SymPy symbols on both parsed expressions and retry an exact, deadline-bounded comparison. Keep equations, sets, and the default grading policy unchanged; validate names and reject malformed contracts.
3. Pass the assumption only from a HARDMath conversion whose audited question establishes it. Coordinate this with the RHS-only HARDMath contract on the `atlas-env-audit` integration branch; main currently converts the whole `ground_truths` field.
4. Add public-API regressions for the three reported regroupings, a wrong exponent, and `\sqrt{x^2}` versus `x` with and without an explicit positive `x`. Replay all 89 affected rows and wrong-answer controls through `verifyit.grade.run`; accept the change only if the supported regroupings score 1, wrong replies remain 0, and no calls reach the deadline. The implementation PR should use `Fixes #11740`.

This spans the grader contract, shared conversion, and an audited dataset release, so it needs a scoped implementation rather than a global comparator change.

## 10/05 Micro210 baseline

Evaluation-only entry for the frozen 10/05 model; this does not introduce a new SFT or RL training recipe.

Micro210 is Marin’s mixed reasoning, knowledge, coding and agentic evaluation suite.
This recipe supports 200 distinct tasks across 20 sources (Tau3 excluded), expanded to 440 assignments, including 100 Pi assignments.

## Model and evaluation policy

Model: [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05/tree/ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6), immutable revision `ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6`. The three runs evaluate this same model in existing region-local storage, with no additional training.

The runtime separately selects [marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools](https://huggingface.co/marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools/tree/3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09), revision `3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09`, with no explicit template override and thinking enabled. The model’s embedded tokenizer provenance is not the selected runtime tools revision.

Current harness: 16 global Harbor slots (four rollout workers × four), one 8 H100 policy worker (TP1/DP8/EP8, max_num_seqs 8) and an independent 8 H100 M3 judge (TP8). Policy/judge caps are 21,600 s; root cap is 25,200 s. Native Pi 0.87; context 65,536, 16,384 generated tokens per turn, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95. Compilation and CUDA graphs remain enabled. comments.body:
🤖 On Canonical Micro210, a constant reply scores above Round 3 on TruthfulQA and GPQA Diamond, and 40% on MMLU-Pro. I graded the 140 prepared answer-only tasks, rebuilt with #11120's `prepare_micro` (sha256 equal to `prepared_rollouts_sha256` in #11686), with Round 3's tokenizer, context and output limits. The five replies of the `trivial_replies` launcher in the open #11222 (empty, `hello`, `0`, `I don't know.`, the prompt repeated) went through `run_evaluation`. Single letters went through the rows' own rollout specs.

| Benchmark | Constant reply | Score (%) | Round 1 | Round 2 | Round 3 | Base | Snowball v0.1 |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TruthfulQA | `\boxed{A}` | 100 | 70 | 80 | 70 | 20 | 90 |
| GPQA Diamond | `B` | 50 | 56.7 | 56.7 | 43.3 | 33.3 | 66.7 |
| MMLU-Pro | `I don't know.` | 40 | 70 | 70 | 60 | 40 | 90 |
| IFBench | `hello` | 10 | 40 | 40 | 30 | 0 | 40 |

The other ten answer benchmarks score 0 for every reply. The six agentic benchmarks were not run.

- TruthfulQA: the generated-choice prompts list the options in `mc2_targets` order, which starts with a true answer. Option A is true in every task: 10 in Micro210, 41 in Mini840, 817 rows of `truthfulqa/truthful_qa`. A seeded shuffle of each task's options would remove this. The full policy's MC2 likelihood scoring does not depend on order.
- MMLU-Pro: without `answer is (X)` or `Answer: X`, the extractor takes the last standalone capital A-J, so `I don't know.` counts as option I, the key of 4 tasks.
- GPQA Diamond: 5 of the 10 drawn keys are B.
- IFBench: the prepared rows grade it with the `evalchemy` wheel of `runtime-v4`, whose IFBench checkers are byte-identical to `vendor/evalchemy` before #10423. In one of the 10 tasks (key 278, the capitals of European countries north of 45°) a correct reply cannot pass: the checker's list leaves out Kyiv, so the 28 correct capitals score 0 and the 27 without Kyiv score 1.

This does not show that a round guesses. On these 10 tasks, the three benchmarks cannot tell a round from a constant below the floor. They carry 8.7 of Round 3's 41.07 points. Without them, Rounds 1-3, the base and Snowball v0.1 average 49.8, 44.7, 38.1, 13.3 and 40.3%.

Launcher floors rerun with `trivial_replies` on #11222's head over a TaskSpec corpus of a benchmark's prepared tasks. The TruthfulQA count needs only the dataset (`uv run --with pyarrow --with huggingface_hub python check.py`):

```python
import base64, json
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

path = hf_hub_download("open-athena/Marin-Micro-Eval-210", "data/validation.parquet", repo_type="dataset",
                       revision="4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819")
labels = []
for row in pq.read_table(path).to_pylist():
    if row["benchmark"] == "truthfulqa":
        files = json.loads(row["task_spec"])["resources"]["verifier"]
        config = json.loads(base64.b64decode(next(f for f in files if f["path"] == "config.json")["source"]["content_base64"]))
        labels.append(config["spec"]["doc"]["mc2_targets"]["labels"][0])
print(f"option A is true in {sum(labels)} of {len(labels)} TruthfulQA tasks")
```

The sole absent trial is `tb2-recovery/terminal-bench/sam-cell-seg`, repetition 1, original UID 268: `VerifierTimeoutError`. It is infrastructure-absent, not a zero. TB2 has 29/30 coverage (96.67%); every benchmark and the complete suite exceed the 90% valid-trial threshold. The final native and raw Harbor error audit found no `AgentTimeoutError`. Native zero rewards for failed task submissions are retained. No trial is imputed.

The uncertainty calculation follows the prior Exp3 seal and [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Each benchmark uses the conservative task-level SEM bound `s = 0.5/sqrt(10*0.9)`, including the 90% valid-trial allowance. With scored fractions `r_b`, means `m_b` and weights `w_b=1/20`, set `mu=sum(w_b*r_b*m_b)`, `delta=sum(w_b*(1-r_b))` and `sigma=sqrt(sum((w_b*r_b*s)^2))`. The Imbens–Manski critical value solves `Phi(c+delta/sigma)-Phi(-c)=0.95`; here `c=1.9381`. The interval is `[mu-c*sigma, mu+c*sigma+delta]`, clipped to [0,1]; benchmark intervals use one cell. Identified bounds assign missing rewards values in [0,1] without sampling uncertainty, so they are not confidence intervals. Repetitions are not independent tasks; these intervals do not measure serving-stack reproducibility.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
TL;DR: Model merging is a promising direction for Marin: different Grug/Snowball checkpoints have complementary strengths, but we do not yet have a reliable way to combine them while preserving the base model's other capabilities. Cheap weight-space operations could make this orders of magnitude less expensive than on-policy distillation (OPD). We would benefit from expert input on how to make that tradeoff work for our mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

The policy evaluation tracker illustrates the problem (percentages; higher is better):

| Checkpoint | MATH500 | GPQA-Diamond | HumanEval+ | NUPA | BFCL-Parity/Pi |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Grug Antidoom Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02) | 95.00 | 67.30 | 72.60 | 0.10 | 5.70 |
| [Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92) | 89.60 | 42.90 | 68.90 | 40.60 | 16.30 |
| [Grug Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04) | 92.60 | 63.00 | 86.60 | 0.30 | 43.90 |

Source: [policy-tracker snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/TRACKER.md). These are policy NUPA scores; the merge study instead optimized NUPA200, a 200-task subset of the policy’s 5,000-task panel. BFCL-Parity/Pi is the policy's tool-use evaluation with the Pi agent. No checkpoint in this comparison achieves the best score in every column.

Our [initial study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) shows both the appeal and the unresolved problem. Static merge construction typically required roughly 1e11–1e12 estimated arithmetic FLOPs per checkpoint, often without GPUs. This supports the prospect of a large compute advantage over OPD, which requires rollout generation and training; we have not run a matched OPD cost comparison. Evaluation and any calibration or expert-selection work add costs beyond static construction.

The best merge scored 36.50% on NUPA200 and 48.78% on BFCL-Parity, versus historical specialist references of 38.00% and 43.90%, respectively. But its recipe copied only 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from the intended Base (Step12). On non-target benchmarks, it scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus Base’s historical policy scores of 95.00% and 67.30%; these were not matched reruns. That study did not establish capability-preserving transfer into Base.

We would welcome advice from people with model-merging experience, especially on transferring specialist behavior into an existing MoE checkpoint with limited weight changes, handling expert/router compatibility and the tokenizer differences observed in #9975, and choosing retention evaluations that expose damage outside the target benchmarks.

Done when: expert feedback informs a concrete follow-up design with a fixed Base, explicit limits on weight changes, and pre-agreed target and non-target evaluation criteria.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The best merge in [#9975](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) scored 36.50% NUPA200 and 48.78% BFCL-Parity, but copied only 0.76% of Base weights unchanged; its lower MATH500 and GPQA-Diamond scores are historical comparisons, not matched retention tests. Changing the loading and tokenizer bundle alone moved BFCL-Parity from 0.81% to 17.07% with NUPA weights fixed, so the earlier search cannot isolate weight transfer. [PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already supplies merging tools, but does not enforce the later 25% change budget; the [earlier follow-up outline](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975#issuecomment-6074700342) belongs here as a Base-anchored study.

**Relevant code**
- [`merge.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/merge.py#L19-L42) — checkpoint export entry point.
- [`select_experts.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py#L19-L56) — ranked and random expert transfers.
- [`evaluation/cli.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — shared evaluation launch path.

# Proposed Fix

1. Pin Step12 as Base and pin both donor revisions. Run matched Base and donor evaluations with identical prompts and decoding; hold Base configuration, tokenizer, chat template, and generation settings fixed for merge candidates, with separate tokenizer and special-token-row controls.
2. After #9974 lands, verify tensor and expert-row alignment, then add an export audit that counts changed scalar positions against Base at stored dtype, globally and by component. Reject any candidate above a 25% change budget; report router, shared-expert, routed-expert, attention, and embedding changes separately.
3. Predeclare 5%, 10%, and 25% budgets and compare Base-anchored activation-ranked NUPA/BFCL expert transfers with matched random-expert and no-transfer controls. Record routing changes and collect fresh activation data because the archive lacks the transcripts needed for exact replay.
4. Freeze NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity as target tests, and MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, and HumanEval+ as retention sentinels; run the full policy cohort on finalists. Agree numeric target gains and maximum retention losses after matched baseline repeats but before candidate scoring, then publish recipes, checkpoint revisions, changed-weight counts, all scores, negative results, and construction/calibration/evaluation costs. Advance a candidate only if both targets improve and every retention floor passes.

Expert feedback requested: Is Base-router compatibility adequately tested by matched activation and routing checks, or should expert alignment use a different control? Are the proposed tokenizer controls and retention sentinels sufficient to detect damage outside NUPA and BFCL?

comments.author: craffel
comments.body:
Hi, I can comment a bit on this (also tagging @marcociccone who has been doing a lot of work along these lines).

Anecdotally it seems that merging may work better* than OPD in the MOPD setup when merging RL-trained checkpoints:
- [This paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12566) which seems to have invented MOPD without credit (?) includes merging as a baseline, where it compares favorably.
- The ["MOPD paper"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30406) includes task arithmetic (a weak merging baseline) where it performs roughly on par with OPD
- The [Open-MOPD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19098) also has some merging results and it works reasonably well.
- [This very recent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04272) also has some promising results with merging in the MOPD setting.
- The fact that merging can work well in the RL setting is explored in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22039).

The trouble is that there is some conflicting evidence, which I think stems from the following:
- We generally do not have a precise characterization of how well merging will work in a particular setting.
- Most work that evaluates merging takes the simplest possible method off the shelf (generally task arithmetic). This can work ok (anecdotally especially for larger models, see [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03617)) but there has been a ton of work on more sophisticated merging methods that have been pretty conclusively demonstrated to work better. The additional trouble, though, is that there are details that people often get wrong, for example how to merge the embedding/unembedding matrices, or other nuisance details (see e.g. the discussion of incorrect implementations of RegMean in [our recent work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01329)).
- Underlying merging is the choice of mixing coefficients for the constituent models, which is rarely explored but turns out to be important in practice.
- To get to the asterisk above, there often is only a cursory notion of what "better" means; often it is found e.g. that merging works better than MT/OPD on some tasks and worse on others, but this seems to largely be a consequence of the implicit mixing weights used by a merging method where no mixing weight tuning is done.

As mentioned above @marcociccone is finishing up a project investigating this much more thoroughly; the end product is a method for tuning merging coefficients and strong results using strong merging methods. It's a bit hard to claim "pareto-optimality" in terms of the merged model dominating the MT/OPD model for *every* task, but merging at the very least seems to be on par and also has the huge advantage of being much cheaper to use (and in particular much cheaper to try out new mixing coefficients to balance capabilities to your preferred profile).

HTH.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Thank you very much @craffel for the detailed comment here! As a Grug-brained newbie in the space of model merging, I would certainly be happy to experiment with the method of @marcociccone if he would like to check something into our monorepo!

Naively, it seems that model merging can produce models that look OK (even strong) under our eval policy but then acquire weird tics / behavioral quirks that would make them pretty unappealing as an official release. So we're looking into how to harden our eval policy against these kinds of failures (and also hopefully get better at merging models)

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 A data point on the transfer losses in #9920 and #9984: both experts were trained on targets that never open a reasoning block, and every distilled arm, and the half-strength merge, carries that shape to prompts outside CRUXEval. That fits the off-target losses better than skill interference does.

**Expert data.** The SFT rows of expert E ([`task133-20261007-prepared-v2`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Transfer-Artifacts-2026.10/tree/98c153c05ddd02068c5415144696e01e9a61c0a2/teacher-traces/cruxeval-test-exposed/task133-20261007-prepared-v2)) and expert E2 ([`task162-e2-prepared-20261009-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Two-Expert-Transfer-Artifacts-2026.10/tree/7a96dade2635b0bd76a1a67cb5381fad2d6b2be8/teacher-traces/mopd2/task162-e2-prepared-20261009-v1)) put the reasoning inline: `reasoning\n<|end_think|>\n\nanswer`. The `chat_template.jinja` shipped with them renders assistant `content` verbatim and ends the generation prompt at the assistant header, so `<|start_think|>` is in neither the prompt nor the target. `MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE` renders reasoning as `<|start_think|>…<|end_think|>` ([`chat_template.py` L109](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f79686b2185c57d2db32569d9c27f2bcebd04e76/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_template.py#L109)).

| SFT rows | rows | with `<\|start_think\|>` | with one `<\|end_think\|>` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| expert E | 1,454 | 0 | 1,454 |
| expert E2 | 1,359 | 0 | 1,359 |

The counts are the same in `train.jsonl` and in the token ids of `train-prebuilt.jsonl.gz`.

**What E learned.** Of E's 12,800 k=8 samples (`task145-e-k8-20261008`), 98 have one well-formed block; 11,133 have no reasoning before the first `<|end_think|>`, 4,747 repeat the opener and 1,679 reopen after closing. The plain and RS-SFT sets are drawn from these samples: none of the 1,503 RS-SFT targets starts with `<|start_think|>`, and 711 contain two or more. For comparison, #10400 finds two or more thinking segments in 1.9% to 9.1% of the thinking messages of Marin's general checkpoints.

**What the arms carry.** Teacher-forced next-token probabilities on 48 prompts (12 each from CRUXEval, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K and IFEval) for the checkpoints #9920 and #9984 pin, averaged over the 36 prompts that are not CRUXEval:

| | B | E | RS-SFT 282 | OPD 75 | plain SFT 399 | mixed RS 727 | MOPD 100 | merge TA0.5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `/think`, after `<\|start_think\|>\n`: next token closes or reopens | 0.0016 | 0.156 | 0.220 | 0.216 | 0.298 | 0.376 | 0.829 | 0.152 |
| `/nothink`: first token is `<\|start_think\|>` | 0.0000 | 0.051 | 0.288 | 0.041 | 0.373 | 0.274 | 0.420 | 0.115 |

On the CRUXEval prompts under `/nothink` the opener probability is 0.95 for RS-SFT and 0.78 for OPD (B 0.00), in line with the think blocks the #9920 and #9984 panels counted in thinking-off CRUXEval replies (28 and 18 of 30; v0.1 0). B itself writes a second opener after `<|start_think|>\n` on the CRUXEval prompt format (0.91, against 0.0015 on the other prompts), so part of the CRUXEval gap that E closes is format.

**Reading.** The off-target losses sit on format-strict benchmarks (BFCL-Parity, NUPA with 62.8% to 71.9% valid format, thinking-off FinanceBench, length-capped TriviaQA), while knowledge and reasoning benchmarks hold. Every expert row has the shape #11706 describes: reasoning without the opener, then `<|end_think|>`. The probe shows that the arms carry it, not that it causes the losses, and how far an arm shifts does not rank its BFCL loss. A direct test: re-score B on the affected benchmarks with the current panel code (B's panel row is from older code), then compare RS282 with RS-SFT on the same samples rewritten into one well-formed block each, and with an expert rebuilt from the GLM traces rendered with the opener. If the format is fixed and the losses stay, the format is not the cause.

issues.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is a human-guided, agent-executed experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

**Start with the [contributor guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_recipe/experiments/belay/CONTRIBUTING.md)**: how to check an idea against the recipe, pick a Track, follow its runs, and take it up the ladder.

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Plans, results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**The usual path for an idea:** optionally a `vanilla-*` Track first, for a radical idea or a stronger signal; then `speedrun`, for fast iteration and to check it fits the current recipe; then `hero-mfu` if it will change MFU a lot; then `ladder`. Maintainers promote ideas into the recipe from those results.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once, at the baseline's step count. After a `hero-mfu` result, each rung's steps are adjusted for the MFU change (better MFU, more steps). Without one, the verdict is provisional: the idea needs a `hero-mfu` result before it joins the recipe | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer runs it | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **[Admin](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#admin)** (maintainers, signed in to Marina): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

Notice: The majority of our compute right now is dedicated to SFT and RL runs. As a result, runs outside the speedrun track may queue up for a couple days.
