comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Test of the intake workflow: this comment should be copied into #9451 after a 👍 from a marin-devs member, and then get a 🚀. (Not a research suggestion.)

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try adding **spelling-normalised byte embeddings** to the input. Each token's input embedding row gets a learned sum over the first 8 UTF-8 bytes of its surface string, one 256 x d table per byte position. Read the bytes after stripping leading spaces and lowercasing, so " The", "the" and "The" share every byte row. Add two small feature rows to keep what the normalisation removes: leading space (0/1) and case (lower, capitalised, all caps, mixed). Zero-init the tables so the model starts identical to the baseline. Add the byte sum to the vocab table before the token gather, so there is no per-token cost and no extra communication. Input side only: do not share byte rows on the lm_head. Keep 8 byte positions and table width d_model at every rung.

Rationale: tokens that are spelling or case variants of each other start with unrelated embeddings and have to learn their similarity from context. Sharing byte rows gives the model that information directly, and it is information the body cannot compute from token ids. This is close to Spelling Bee Embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18030); the space/case normalisation is the addition.

comments.author: xTimeCrystal
comments.body: Track: speedrun Similar to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08888, try implementing a Full Bandwidth Transformer (FBT): the trunk runs K parallel passes over the sequence, and pass p's input at token t is fused from that token's embedding and the previous pass's output at token t-1: `x^{(p)}_{t} = norm(x_t + W_fuse norm(h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}))` - Use this formula, not the paper's. This is more stable. - `x_t` is the pass-1 input of token t (its embedding). - `h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}` is the final layer's output of pass `p-1` at position `t-1` (what the LM head reads), not that pass's input. - `norm` is parameter-free RMSNorm. - `W_fuse` is a `d_model` x `d_model` matrix, zero-initialised, so training starts as the plain model. - Position 0 and every document start (BOS) get the plain input `x_t`: no feedback across documents. - Gradients flow through all passes; do not detach or no-grad any pass. - Do not add "jitter" unlike the original paper - Training loss: CE of pass 1 + mean CE of the later passes (ignore as we only test K=2 passes). Evaluation: the last pass only. Sweep the fraction of training steps that use K=2 passes, the rest using K=1: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 (always 2 passes). Never use K=3. Evaluate every run with K=2. Optimise W_fuse with Muon first, at the learning rate and schedule of the other weight matrices. Then sweep 0.7x and 1.4x to bracket the optimal W_fuse lr using Muon. Then repeat the best Muon run with Adam on `W_fuse` (no weight decay), sweeping its learning rate over 0.7x, 1x, 1.4x. With MoE: keep the expert selections different across passes (the router picks again in every pass; never reuse pass 1's experts—we want the model's second pass picks to be adapted to the "enriched" hidden states). Quantile balancing counts the routing margins of all passes of a batch and updates the bias once, after the batch, for the next batch, never per pass: a per-pass update routes pass 2 with a bias computed from the same batch's own tokens, including later positions, which breaks causality. Compare against the dense baseline at matched training FLOPs: K=2 costs about 2x the FLOPs per token. Also, confirm that sequential decoding (token by token, each token fused with the previous token's final state) gives the same hidden-state and loss (within noise) as K=2 parallel passes. In our nanochat run they agreed to within 0.0003 bpb. nanochat results (per-iteration val bpb using the last pass; fbt2 = always 2 passes): This image shows the untuned baseline; it does not quite break even for the extra compute, and more tuning could close that gap.

comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Exact-match pointer mixture on the output with 8 candidates. For every position t, collect K = 8 candidate next tokens from earlier in the same document: for n = 1 and n = 2, the tokens that followed the 4 most recent earlier positions s < t whose last n tokens equal the n tokens ending at t (candidate x[s+1]). Mix them into the output: p(y) = (1 - G) p_vocab(y) + open * sum_k pi_k [c_k = y], where (pi_0, pi_1..pi_K) = softmax(0, l_1..l_K) over the candidates that exist, l_k = h . w_k + 8 * b[k, a_k] - 2 with h the lm_head input and a_k the number of other slots proposing the same token, G = open * sum_k pi_k, open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1). w [d_model, 8], b [8, 8] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M the pointer mass on the label. Implementation: find the matches with integer work on the token ids only, per sequence: sort (document id, key, position) with key = token for n = 1 and previous_token * vocab + token for n = 2, take the sorted neighbour as the previous match and follow those links three more times for the older matches, then gather x[s+1]; batch the sorts over rows. Take ce from the existing fused cross-entropy kernel with per-token reduction; no second pass over the vocabulary, no logit gather, no [B, S, vocab] tensor. Target step time within 1% of the control. Same settings at every rung.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Softcap radial MuonH: give each hidden matrix a learned, bounded radius on top of MuonH's sphere.

(Generated by an automated research harness. Edited to replace the earlier evidence with the completed results; bottom line first.)

**Bottom line**
- On Belay's 8-minute d512 speedrun, softcap beats the recipe's MuonH beyond the 0.005 band (below).
- That edge shrinks with size: on Belay's ladder recipe it is inside the band by d768 (one seed).
- Softcap does **not** beat a fairly tuned MuonW-family baseline. Once MuonW gets a tuned head LR and schedule-scaled decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), that baseline matches or beats softcap.
- So we are not proposing softcap as a ladder improvement on current evidence. d1024/d1280 are still running.

**Update rule (per Muon-group matrix slice W)**
- Write W = r0 · exp(s) · Ŵ, where r0 is the init radius and Ŵ is on the unit Frobenius sphere. Ŵ takes the usual MuonH hyperball step.
- s (a scalar log-radius per slice) is stepped by Adam on the radial gradient g = <∂L/∂W, W>, at the same LR and schedule as the matrix LR.
- Bound: outward steps are scaled by (1 − (s/c)²) and inward steps are taken in full. With c = 2 the radius is capped at e² ≈ 7.4× init.
- Slices whose output passes through a scale-removing norm keep a fixed radius (plain MuonH). Head and fallback groups are unchanged.

**d512 speedrun (Belay recipe, same-commit MuonH control)**
- Equal data, six paired GB200 seeds: softcap − MuonH mean −0.0083, one-sided 95% upper bound −0.0059, 6/6 seeds better. Three H100 seeds agree (mean −0.0082).
- An equal-time check gave smaller margins on the seeds read (about −0.004).
- learnable_qk_mult adds nothing (control + lqk +0.0002). The radius gain does transfer under the recipe's MLA q/k norms.

**Ladder (Belay recipe, one seed per rung; single-run gaps under 0.005 are ties)**
- Against MuonH: d512 −0.0103 (seed 1; −0.0057 on seed 0), d768 −0.0030 (a tie).
- Against the best MuonW-family run (MuonC, head LR ×0.35): d512 tie (−0.0025 on averaged reruns), d768 −0.0049 (a tie at the band edge).
- Same-seed reruns of identical settings at d512 differ by up to about 0.003, so one-seed margins below the band carry little weight.

**KMA d768 target (where the method was developed)**
- Softcap leads MuonW tuned on LR and decays by −0.0044 (seeds 2-11, held-out agreeing).
- That MuonW was under-tuned:
  - With MuonW's AdamW head LR tuned as well (×0.25-0.5), the lead drops to about −0.002, inside noise.
  - MuonC with a tuned head (2.4944, seed 0) beats every weight-normalized variant we tried, including softcap's best (2.5013).

**What we learned**
- Weight-normalized radial MuonH's apparent edge over MuonW came mostly from two things a fair MuonW also gets:
  - the AdamW head LR being too large;
  - plain decoupled decay shrinking the matrices late.
- MuonC's scheduled decay fixes the second, which matches the paper's prediction (flat late weight norm, bounded grad/weight ratio).

Gate logits l_n = h . w_n + 8 * b_n * log2(1 + c_n) / 12 - 2 for n = 1, 2, where h is the lm_head input; (pi_0, pi_1, pi_2) = softmax(0, l_1, l_2) over the orders with c_n > 0; open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1); G = open * (pi_1 + pi_2). comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

At each step of training, we estimate the gradient against the 'weights', where the weights is a weighted sum over all prior gradients. However this weighted sum has a restricted set of options because we only modify it via new_update + modifier*all_prior_updates. A richer set is possible. Try this:

Implement linear init removal in our Hyperball optimizer. For every weight matrix Hyperball constrains (attention and MLP matrices; leave embeddings and norm gains alone), keep a scalar b, the coefficient of the initial weights W₀ in the current weights. It starts at 1.0. Regenerate W₀ from the init seed rather than storing a copy. On every step, keep b updated as b ← a·b, where a = R/‖W − ηV‖ is Hyperball’s projection factor. From step N/3 to step 2N/3, subtract a fixed amount of the init before projecting: W ← W − ηV − d·W₀ with d = min(δ, b), then project back to radius R, and update b ← a·(b − d). Pick δ so b reaches exactly 0 at step 2N/3. A good start is δ ≈ b(N/3) divided by the number of steps in the window, then adjust slightly to account for the shrinking from projection. Outside that window the optimizer is unchanged.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**Learned-radius MuonH (nonsi) plus an s(t)² head and late-matrix anneal.** This changes only the optimizer. It adds one scalar per matrix slice and no model change.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule):
1. *Learned radius ("nonsi").* Write each MuonH-group slice as W = r0 · exp(ρ) · Ŵ, with r0 = ‖W‖_F at init and Ŵ on the unit sphere.
   - Ŵ takes MuonH's hyperball step, unchanged.
   - ρ (one scalar per slice) is stepped by Adam (β 0.9 / 0.99) on the radial gradient ⟨∂L/∂W, W⟩, at the matrix LR and its usual (unannealed) schedule. There is no cap.
   - Slices whose output feeds a norm through linear maps only (so ⟨∂L/∂W, W⟩ = 0) keep ρ = 0, i.e. plain MuonH. These are the MLA kv down-projection (w_dkv), the MLA query (w_q) and key up-projection (w_uk), and the MoE latent down-projection (w_latent_down). The KDA write-strength group learns ρ at its own LR.
2. *Head anneal.* The lm_head / output_proj (AdamH) LR becomes lr_max · s(t)² instead of lr_max · s(t).
3. *Late matrix anneal.* From step t₀ = round(0.7937 · N), multiply the MuonH matrix LR by s(t) / s(t₀), so the angular step falls as s(t)² from there and is continuous at t₀.

The Adam groups are unchanged. With ρ ≡ 0 and both anneals off, this is the recipe.

**Evidence** (our own runs, Paloma macro loss)

*8-minute d512 speedrun, equal data, 6 paired seeds, against a same-commit recipe MuonH control (mean 3.0423):*

| Arm | Δ vs MuonH |
|---|---|
| nonsi + s² anneals (this) | **−0.0115** (all 6 seeds; one-sided 95% bound −0.0098) |
| nonsi without the anneals | −0.0079 |
| MuonC (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), λ 0.1, + the same anneals | −0.0033 |
| MuonC, λ 0.2, + the same anneals | −0.0161 |

*d512 on the ladder recipe (10,767 steps), seed 1:* this 2.8518; recipe MuonH 2.8697 (+0.018); nonsi without the anneals 2.8604 (+0.009).

**Caveats**
- A tuned MuonC with the same anneals beats this on the speedrun: at λ 0.2 it is 0.0046 better (five of six seeds). The anneals are not specific to the learned radius.
- On the larger ladder rungs, the same anneals helped our capped variant (softcap) less and less: −0.008 at d512, −0.010 at d768, −0.004 at d1024, and +0.006 (worse) at d1280. nonsi with the anneals at d768 to d1280 is still running.

comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**MuonC with an s(t)² head and late-matrix anneal.** This replaces MuonH's sphere with Muon plus schedule-scaled weight decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), and adds the two anneals from our nonsi intake above. It changes only the optimizer, with no new parameters.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps):
1. *Matrix LR with a late anneal.* lr_m(t) = lr_t until t₀ = round(0.7937 · N), then lr_m(t) = lr_t · s(t) / s(t₀). The angular step falls as s(t)² from t₀ and is continuous there.
2. *MuonC matrices.* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrix takes W ← W − lr_m(t) · (O + λ_t W), with no projection to a sphere.
   - O is the Muon direction MuonH already computes: Newton–Schulz with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - λ_t = λ · lr_m(t) / lr_max, with λ = 0.2.
   - KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR multiple.
3. *Head.* lm_head / output_proj use AdamW instead of AdamH, at LR lr_max · s(t)², with decoupled decay 0.05.
4. *Adam groups.* They keep their recipe LRs, with AdamW decay 0.05 on rank ≥ 2 leaves, replacing the recipe's annealed gate/router decay.

This differs from X0243/X0244 in the two anneals, the AdamW head, and the decay schedule λ · lr_t / lr_max. Both parts matter on the speedrun. At λ 0.1 the anneals are worth 0.006, and raising λ to 0.2 adds another 0.013.

**Evidence** (our own runs, Paloma macro loss)

*8-minute d512 speedrun, equal data, 6 paired seeds, against a same-commit recipe MuonH control (mean 3.0423):*

| Arm | Δ vs MuonH |
|---|---|
| MuonC λ 0.2 + anneals (this) | **−0.0161** (better on all 6 seeds, −0.011 to −0.020) |
| MuonC λ 0.4 + anneals | −0.0135 |
| MuonC λ 0.1 + anneals | −0.0033 |
| MuonC λ 0.1, no anneals | +0.0025 |
| nonsi + the same anneals (our other intake) | −0.0115 |

λ was picked on these seeds from a grid of λ (0.025 to 0.4) and LR multiplier (0.5× to 1.41×). λ 0.2 and 0.4 are close, and both beat λ 0.1 by far more than picking the best grid cell would add by chance. Every LR change was worse. λ 0.8 is still running.

*Belay ladder recipe, seed 1, λ 0.1 (not yet tuned on the ladder) + anneals vs recipe MuonH:*

| Rung | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Δ | −0.013 | −0.009 | −0.010 | −0.010 |

This was the best run on every rung we measured. A λ sweep on the ladder (0.2 to 0.4 at d512 and d768) is starting.

- The ladder numbers are one seed per rung, with seed-to-seed spread of about 0.003–0.006 in paired gaps.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: ladder

**Law-cap ball: MuonH's matrices take a plain Muon step inside a per-layer Frobenius ball whose radius comes from a closed-form law, plus the s(t)² head anneal and late matrix anneal from our earlier intakes.** There is no weight decay and nothing to tune per rung. The change is optimizer-only, with no new parameters.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps)
1. *Matrices.* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength slice W takes W′ = W − η_t U. If ‖W′‖_F exceeds cap_l, W′ is rescaled onto the ball; otherwise it is kept as is. There is no decay and no projection inside the ball.
   - U is the Muon direction MuonH already computes: Newton–Schulz with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - η_t is the recipe's MuonH LR. From t₀ = round(0.7937 · N) it is multiplied by s(t)/s(t₀) (late anneal). KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR.
   - A slice is a 2-D leaf, or one layer of a stacked leaf.
2. *Cap, from shape and peak LR only.*
   - cap_l = κ · |U_l|, where |U_l| = √(n · min(in, out) · max(1, out/in)) is the Frobenius norm of an orthogonalized update for that slice, and n is the number of matrices in the slice.
   - κ = √(τ · lr_max / (2λ)), with τ = 39 and λ = 0.2. This is the size MuonC's matrices settle at for decay λ (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285). The ball reaches it directly instead of decaying toward it.
3. *Head.* The recipe's AdamH head, with LR lr_max · s(t)² instead of lr_max · s(t).
4. *Adam groups.* Unchanged.

**Evidence** (our own runs on the Belay ladder recipe, seed 1, Paloma macro loss)

| Rung | this | recipe MuonH | Δ | MuonC (λ 0.1) + same anneals, same commit | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 2.8538 | 2.8697 | −0.016 | 2.8569 | −0.003 |
| d768 | 2.6051 | 2.6148 | −0.010 | 2.6062 | −0.001 |
| d1024 | 2.4045 | 2.4075 | −0.003 | 2.3997 | +0.005 |
| d1280 | 2.2627 | 2.2749 | −0.012 | 2.2656 | −0.003 |

- The matrices sit on their caps from early in training. A checkpoint check confirmed this on every rung.
- The cap level is bracketed around the law. At d512, 0.5× and 1.4× the law's cap are clearly worse, and 0.7× ties. At d768, 0.7× is worse and 1.4× is within noise.
- On the 8-minute d512 speedrun (6 seeds) it ties tuned MuonC + the same anneals (+0.0004 vs λ 0.4).

**Caveats**
- One seed per rung. Seed-to-seed spread of paired gaps is about 0.003–0.006, and a second d1280 seed has been proposed.
- It ties, rather than beats, a tuned MuonC with the same anneals (our other intake). Its appeal is that it gets there with no decay to tune: the cap is set from shape and peak LR alone, and the same formula was used at every rung.
- It also avoids a failure we saw with a learned-radius variant (softcap + the same anneals), which fell 0.016 behind at d1280.

comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: ladder

X0250 4 rung scaling ladder with a per-rung matrix decay. This replaces our earlier X0250 ladder request (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-7029815277); please run this one instead of that one.

Keep X0250 exactly at every rung except the matrix decay lambda in lambda_t = lambda * lr_m(t) / lr_max. Instead of the constant 0.2, set lambda per rung so the total matrix decay over the run, lambda * lr_max * N, stays at its d512-rung value: lambda_rung = 0.2 * (lr_max_d512 * N_d512) / (lr_max_rung * N_rung), where lr_max is the rung's MuonH-group peak LR and N its number of steps. d512 keeps 0.2; larger rungs get smaller lambda. This holds the weights' decay timescale at a fixed fraction of training, and it matches the MuonC decay optima WhenWen measured on this ladder (0.2 at d512, about 0.1 at d768; #11785). Everything else is X0250's at every rung: the MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrices step W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with no sphere projection and the late matrix anneal from t0 = round(0.7937 * N); lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2 from that rung's head peak; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W from that rung's Adam peak; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No new parameters or state.

comments.body:
🤖

Track: custom

Rerun the recipe with no flag on competitive-d1024 and competitive-d1280 from this week's branch (seed 0, each Track's own command). Then judge finished ladders against the mean of that run and the s7n run at each rung.

Every competitive rung compares a variant with one finished run (`s7n-d1024`, `s7n-d1280L16`). `belay_s7.py` says the s7n runs were trained on `marin_belay_v1_fp8quality` at `a5a8647840`, which is not an ancestor of the weekly branches. The registry still labels these baselines "(same commit, seed 0)", from the template in `registry_entry.py` line 257.

To first order, `ladder_projection` gives Δ_hero = −0.533·Δd512 − 0.115·Δd768 + 0.434·Δd1024 + 0.980·Δd1280. This reproduces the six recorded projections. A baseline offset at d1280 therefore passes almost fully into every ladder's verdict.

In the six finished ladders (X0014, X0073, X0221, X0226, X0235, X0237), the mean Δ is −0.0134, −0.0093, −0.0079 and −0.0010 from d512 to d1280. From d1024 to d1280, Δ moves toward zero in all six (mean +0.0069); from d768 to d1024 it moves +0.0014. The seed-1 recipe runs in #11785 are +0.0016, +0.0027, −0.0031 and +0.0043 relative to s7n, with the same signs at d1024 and d1280. Measured against them, the d1280 drop disappears and every projection moves by −0.0017. #11785 also found that an apparent d512 lead of −0.0045 was cross-commit noise once rerun on the same commit; the s7n baselines are cross-commit by construction.

A d1280 rerun 0.003 or more above 2.2706 would mean that every ladder's d1280 Δ is biased toward a loss by that amount. A rerun within 0.001 of it rules this out. The d1280 rung also differs from d1024 in batch (1,024 sequences, the hero's tokens per step), steps (20,023 against 39,210) and depth (16 layers), so the rerun separates the baseline from those changes.

Budget: two runs, about 1,010 minutes on one node (d1024) and 1,003 minutes on four nodes (d1280), using the run times on the Belay page.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Builds of the patched PJRT wheel in `marin-community/xla` cache `~/.cache/bazel` wholesale, about 11.6 GB against GitHub's documented 10 GB per-repository limit. Retention is unpredictable, and the difference is 1m35s of build time versus 3h31m.

| run | restore | build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [33013385685](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33013385685) | 3m38s | 1m35s |
| [33093433428](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33093433428) | 0s, nothing to restore | 3h31m33s |

A save at 2026-08-26T21:12Z was gone by the next build at 2026-08-27T16:29Z, which then paid a full cold compile. A save at 2026-08-27T20:04Z is still present a day later. Both entries are the same size, so exceeding the cap does not by itself explain which one survives.

The cached directory holds more than compile output. `external/` and `cache/repos/` carry fetched repositories including the CUDA 13 redistributables, which cost minutes to download again, while `execroot/.../bazel-out` carries the object files that cost hours to rebuild. No size breakdown has been taken, so which part dominates the 11.6 GB is unknown, and that is the first thing needed.

Impact is bounded. Builds run only on pushes to `main` that touch the wheel, so this costs 3½ hours on a refresh or a build-script change, not on routine work. Promotion runs from a published candidate and never compiles.

Done when:

- a size breakdown of the bazel output base is recorded from a build that runs anyway
- the cached content is small enough to be retained between consecutive builds
- two consecutive builds restore the cache, and the second compiles in minutes rather than hours

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body: By default Coreweave treats all pods as critical. We can provide hints for non-critical jobs with a CKS label as noted above. Let's adjust Iris to set these as appropriate. Certainly BATCH jobs can be interruptable (sic), INTERACTIVE we could also use interruptible or graceful-interruptible.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + actionability check
- [x] Locate pod-manifest label stamping and priority bands
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PR/issue)
- [ ] Confirm exact CKS label key + values (blocked on screenshot content)
- [ ] Implement band→CKS-hint mapping + test

# Research

Iris task pods carry no CoreWeave workload-criticality hint, so CKS treats every pod as critical and won't drain them for node maintenance/reclamation. Pods are built one-per-attempt in `_build_pod_manifest`; the priority band (`PRODUCTION`/`INTERACTIVE`/`BATCH`) is already resolved there and drives the Kueue priority class and native `priorityClassName`, so it's the natural key for a criticality hint. The `cks.coreweave.cloud/` prefix is already used at the node level (`SYSTEM_CRITICAL_LABEL`).

**Relevant code**
- [`backends/k8s/tasks.py#L888-L917`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L888-L917) — pod `labels`; `effective_band` resolved here
- [`backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1019-L1021`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1019-L1021) — band → native `priorityClassName`
- [`job.proto#L614-L617`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L614-L617) — `PRIORITY_BAND_{PRODUCTION,INTERACTIVE,BATCH}`
- [`platforms/k8s/constants.py#L16-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/constants.py#L16-L25) — existing CoreWeave `interruptable` toleration
- [`platforms/k8s/nodepool_manifests.py#L15`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/nodepool_manifests.py#L15) — node-level `cks.coreweave.cloud/system-critical`

# Proposed Fix

Stamp a CKS pod-criticality label in the `_build_pod_manifest` `labels` dict, keyed off `effective_band`:

| Band | Hint |
|------|------|
| `PRODUCTION` | critical (default — omit label) |
| `INTERACTIVE` | graceful-interruptible |
| `BATCH` | interruptible |

Define the label key/values as constants next to `COREWEAVE_INTERRUPTABLE_TOLERATION`. Test: assert the manifest label per band via the existing k8s pod-manifest test.

**Blocking question:** the exact CKS label key and its value strings live only in the screenshot, which I can't fetch (auth-gated attachment) or confirm via web search from here. Please confirm before I implement — specifically the label key (e.g. `cks.coreweave.cloud/<?>`) and whether the values are `critical` / `interruptable` / `graceful-interruptible`. This is a production-scheduling label, so I won't guess it.

This is a new scheduling feature touching live CoreWeave behavior, so per policy I'm posting analysis for review rather than opening a PR up front.

comments.body:
### Slurm wrapper used by every command in this issue

All commands submit `run_gpu.sh` from `$WORK/marin` on the AMD HPC Fund cluster. It turns XLA command buffers off; a later `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=...` in `XLA_FLAGS` overrides that. It will be committed to the repo; this comment is the reference until then.

<details><summary>run_gpu.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -o pipefail
cd "$WORK/marin"
export RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=${RAGGED_DOT_IMPL:-xla} PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Command buffers (HIP graphs) corrupt memory on this ROCm stack: nan gradients and segfaults after a few steps.
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer= $XLA_FLAGS"
uv run --no-sync python "$@" 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered -v -E "rocm_pcie_bandwidth|rocm_executor"
```

</details>

🤖

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

comments.body:
🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,229 TFLOP/s in JAX by kernel time (53% of datasheet peak, 97% of PyTorch's sustained 1,261)

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421), 6b47d18 (JAX 454529), 370d41d (JAX 454561), 704ceff (JAX 454577-454580) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt and rocBLAS; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every rocBLAS and hipBLASLt solution per shape and keeps the fastest) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load. It times each `torch.mm` with GPU events recorded just before and after the call, so its rates count kernel time only.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. It runs under `rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` and reports two rates per shape. Kernel time divides the FLOPs by the GPU time of the kernels inside each window, which matches MAMF-finder's timing. Wall clock divides them by host time, which also counts host dispatch and the idle GPU time between calls. Both are sustained rates, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare with.

Hardware and theoretical peaks:

| | MI350X | MI300X |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture, compute units | gfx950, 256 CUs | gfx942, 304 CUs |
| Memory per GPU (as torch reports it) | 288 GB HBM3E (294,896 MB) | 192 GB HBM3 (196,592 MB) |
| Dense bf16 and fp16 peak | 2,307 TFLOP/s, as in this issue (brochure: 2,309.6) | 1,307 TFLOP/s (datasheet: 1,307.4) |
| Node, Slurm partition | k007-002, `mi3508x` | k002-003, `mi3008x` |

The peaks are AMD's dense figures without structured sparsity. `lib/fray/src/fray/device_flops.py` stores the brochure values; the percentages below use 2,307 and 1,307 to match the tables above.

Software, identical on both GPUs:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| ROCm user-space libraries | `rocm==10.0.0` wheels (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-libraries`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx942`, `rocm-sdk-device-gfx950`) from `https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/` |
| hipBLASLt, rocBLAS | 100401-8d1ae90e, 5.6.0.8d1ae90e (from TunableOp's results file) |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, with `amd-torch-device-gfx942` and `-gfx950` 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0. `torch.version.hip` is 7.15.26333 and `torch.version.cuda` is None: a ROCm build, no CUDA |
| JAX | jax and jaxlib 0.11.0, `jax_rocm10_plugin` and `jax_rocm10_pjrt` 0.11.0+rocm10.0.0 |
| Kernel tracing | `rocprofv3` from the `rocm-sdk-core` 10.0.0 wheel |
| MAMF-finder | commit [0359db8](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), benchmark version 4, auto search, default tuning |
| Python, OS | 3.12.12, Linux 5.14.0-611.54.1.el9_7 |
| JAX flags | `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`; the Triton-off run adds `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` |

Each run used GPU 0 while the other 7 GPUs on the node were idle.

```bash
sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/mamf.sbatch --dtype bfloat16"
cluster "cd agents/<name> && sbatch --export=ALL,MARIN_COMMIT=$sha -p mi3508x -w <node> -t 60 -J <name> \
  -o \$WORK/agents/<name>/logs/%x-%j.out experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/jax_matmul.sbatch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --m-range 4096 20480 4096 --n-range 4096 20480 4096 --k-range 4096 20480 4096 \
  --shapes-file experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt"
```

Results in TFLOP/s per GPU, with the share of the dense peak. Shapes are MxNxK. The JAX column is kernel time, with the traced wall-clock rate of the same shape in parentheses.

| GPU | dtype | MAMF (PyTorch) | MSMF (PyTorch) | JAX best | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI350X | bf16 | 1,445 (62.6%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 (54.7%) @ 4608x4096x7168 | 1,229 (53.3%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,178) | 453328, 454577 |
| MI350X | fp16 | 1,377 (59.7%) @ 4096x4096x20480 | 1,177 (51.0%) @ 8192x4096x14336 | 1,086 (47.1%) @ 4096x4096x12288 (wall 1,047) | 453329, 454578 |
| MI300X | bf16 | 698 (53.4%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | 645 (49.3%) @ 6144x4864x8192 | not run | 453334 |

The JAX column covers a 125-shape grid (M, N and K each 4096, 8192, ..., 20480), the June model's projection shapes, and, for bf16, the 28 shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted (job 454579). By kernel time, JAX reaches 97% of MSMF in bf16 and 92% in fp16. Without the tracer, the best bf16 wall-clock rate was 1,192 at 4096x4096x16384 and 1,180 at 4096x4096x12288 (job 453420).

Measured against these ceilings instead of the datasheet, the MI350X baseline above (3.88% MFU, 90 TFLOP/s per GPU) runs at 7.3% of the JAX bf16 kernel-time ceiling. The confirmed MI300X batch-16 row (8.66%, 113 TFLOP/s) runs at 17.5% of PyTorch's MSMF; JAX was not measured on MI300X.

The MI300X run reproduces the MI300X bf16 row in [Stas Bekman's table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (MAMF 676, MSMF 659, PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0): MAMF is 3.3% higher and MSMF 2.1% lower. His table has no MI350X row. His MI355X row reads 62.6% of peak, the same share as our MI350X MAMF.

The next table times the same matmul shapes in both frameworks, in bf16 on MI350X, using the shapes MAMF-finder shortlisted. MSMF is PyTorch's sustained rate after TunableOp has kept the fastest rocBLAS or hipBLASLt solution for that shape; the TunableOp column names the library it picked. JAX kernel time comes from job 454579, where XLA's autotuner picked a hipBLASLt kernel for every shape. JAX wall clock comes from job 453412, which ran without the tracer.

| Shape | MSMF | TunableOp | JAX kernel | JAX / MSMF, kernel | JAX wall | JAX / MSMF, wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4608x4096x7168 | 1,261 | rocBLAS | 1,052 | 83% | 1,008 | 80% |
| 4096x4096x8192 | 1,246 | hipBLASLt | 1,209 | 97% | 1,150 | 92% |
| 3584x4608x8192 | 1,237 | rocBLAS | 1,199 | 97% | 1,137 | 92% |
| 4096x4096x20480 | 1,224 | hipBLASLt | 1,179 | 96% | 1,153 | 94% |
| 4096x2048x20480 | 1,089 | hipBLASLt | 1,111 | 102% | 1,065 | 98% |
| 2048x4096x4096 | 1,080 | rocBLAS | 959 | 89% | 828 | 77% |

An earlier version of this comment read the 2-23% wall-clock gap as XLA choosing slower kernels. Most of that gap was the timing method. Wall clock counts host dispatch and the GPU's idle time between calls: on MI350X a trivial jitted op takes about 43 µs to dispatch, and the GPU idles about 12-15 µs between executions even when the host keeps ahead (job 454529). Kernel time removes that overhead. On 2048x4096x4096 it moves JAX from 77% to 89% of MSMF, and on 4096x4096x8192 from 92% to 97%. JAX's kernels are within 4% of MSMF on four shapes. Two gaps remain: 17 points on 4608x4096x7168 and 11 points on 2048x4096x4096. TunableOp picked a rocBLAS solution for both. Every GEMM kernel XLA picked in these runs carries hipBLASLt's `UserArgs` naming, and we have not checked whether XLA's autotuner considers rocBLAS solutions or whether they account for those gaps. TunableOp also picked rocBLAS for 3584x4608x8192, where JAX's hipBLASLt kernel reaches 97%.

On MI350X in bf16, the June model's projection GEMMs at 4096 tokens per GPU run at 369 TFLOP/s (k and v weight gradients, 2560x640x4096) to 1,058 (lm head weight gradient) by kernel time through JAX (job 454577). 4096x2560x2560 is the shape of the q, attention output and shared expert gate, up and down projections, and of their input gradients. It runs at 972 by kernel time and 826 by untraced wall clock (job 454529). The lm head forward runs at 1,030 by kernel time and 1,029 by untraced wall clock. The k and v projections, 4096x640x2560, run at 427 by kernel time with XLA's Triton GEMM and at 556 with hipBLASLt (next table). By untraced wall clock they run at 257 with Triton. Full list in [`snowball_shapes.txt`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/63b08883fd1c77de655310ef7c050950533b69a9/experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/snowball_shapes.txt). The routed-expert `ragged_dot` and the small router, attention gate and GatedNorm GEMMs are not covered.

In bf16, XLA generates its own Triton GEMM for four of the k and v shapes: every shape with a dimension of 640, and 2560x1280x4096. Every other shape uses a hipBLASLt kernel. With `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` (job 454580), XLA uses hipBLASLt for these shapes too, and its kernels run 17-33% faster in bf16. Kernel time in TFLOP/s:

| Shape | Use | Triton (454577) | hipBLASLt, Triton off (454580) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096x640x2560 | k and v projections | 427 | 556 | +30% |
| 2560x640x4096 | k and v weight gradients | 369 | 490 | +33% |
| 2560x1280x4096 | k and v weight gradients, fused | 514 | 664 | +29% |
| 4096x2560x640 | k and v input gradients | 471 | 552 | +17% |

Of the other 38 shapes in the Triton-off run, 33 used the same hipBLASLt kernel as with Triton on, and their kernel time moved by at most 1.6%. For the other 5, the autotuner picked a different hipBLASLt kernel in the new run (see the variation note). Under the tracer, wall clock moved the other way on the four Triton shapes: on 4096x640x2560 a call took 48 µs with Triton and 61 µs with hipBLASLt, against kernel times of 31 and 24 µs, so host-side work sets the wall-clock rate at this size. We have not measured these shapes with Triton off without the tracer. In fp16 (job 454578), XLA also picks Triton for 4096x2560x1280; we did not run fp16 with Triton off.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- fp16 is slower than bf16 for dense matmuls on MI350X: MAMF is 5% lower, JAX 12% lower by kernel time.
- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,179 and 1,229 TFLOP/s by kernel time (job 454577).
- Run-to-run variation on k007-002. With the same kernel, repeated runs agree closely: across the 24 MAMF shapes where jobs 454579 and 454580 ran the same kernel, the median difference is 0.3% and the largest 0.6%. Some shapes move more. 4096x4096x16384 measured 1,188, 1,221 and 1,189 by kernel time (jobs 454529, 454561, 454577), and 1,192 and 1,153 by untraced wall clock (jobs 453420, 454529). Treat differences of about 3% as noise. XLA's autotuner can also pick a different hipBLASLt kernel for the same shape in a new run. It did so for 4 of the 28 MAMF shapes between jobs 454579 and 454580 and moved three of them by 7-12% (for example 20480x4096x12288: 1,039 with a 192x320 tile in job 454579, 1,164 with a 256x256 tile in job 454580).
- Under `rocprofv3`, wall clock reads lower for shapes that take less than about 100 µs per call, because the tracer adds host work to every dispatch: 4096x1280x2560 reads 401 traced (job 454561) and 472-550 in two untraced passes (job 454529). Wall-clock numbers above say which kind they are.
- The node matters. JAX on MAMF-finder's 28 shapes ran a median of 3% faster on k007-002 than on k007-004 by wall clock, and faster on 26 of the 28 shapes (jobs 453412 and 453338). The two slower shapes, 20480x4096x12288 (-8%) and 16384x8192x8192 (-4%), may reflect XLA's autotuner picking a different kernel rather than the node: 1,043 on k007-002 matches the 192x320-tile kernel in the variation note, and these two runs did not record kernel names. k007-001 and k007-003 have not been compared. The bf16 grid's best wall-clock rate was 1,156 on k007-004 (job 453314) against 1,192 on k007-002.
- With `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`, JAX ran bf16 matmuls at 15-17 TFLOP/s, 1% of the autotuned rate (job 453316, stopped by its 45-minute limit after 99 shapes). Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The MI350X MAMF and MSMF runs (jobs 453328 and 453329) predate the fix in stas00/ml-engineering#143, so their power and clock readings, the 38 MHz and 308 W in their logs, and the "not a boost burst" warning from the MAMF boost check all come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86%, JAX by kernel time on the same shape (1,189 in job 454577) about 81%, and JAX by untraced wall clock in job 453523 (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.
- Next: measure a training step with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false` to see whether the faster hipBLASLt kernels for the k and v GEMMs carry over. Separately, check whether XLA can use the rocBLAS solutions TunableOp picked for 4608x4096x7168 and 2048x4096x4096 (`tunableop-*.csv` in the results directory), and whether those solutions close the remaining gaps.

</details>

Edit: first posted with JAX numbers from node k007-004 while MAMF-finder ran on k007-002. All MI350X numbers now come from k007-002. JAX medians now use the true median of the ten windows. The MI350X telemetry note was corrected after jobs 453520 and 453523 showed MAMF-finder sampling a different GPU. Second edit: JAX now reports kernel time from a `rocprofv3` trace next to wall clock, and comparisons with MAMF and MSMF use kernel time (jobs 454577-454580). This corrects the earlier reading that the wall-clock gap came from XLA's kernel choice; XLA's choice still costs 17-33% on the k and v shapes, where it picks its own Triton GEMM. The Snowball shapes now cover separate k and v projections, the k and v weight gradients and the input gradients, and the paragraph names every projection behind a shared shape. Added the Triton-off comparison, the run-to-run variation note, and the TunableOp library choices. Scripts moved to `experiments/amd/matmul_ceiling/`, and the grid arguments are now `--m-range`, `--n-range` and `--k-range`.

Commit: 8471641 (local, not pushed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 453565 (A/B), 453564 (microbenchmark), baseline 453384

PR: #9859 (AMD Instinct only; NVIDIA, TPU and megablox unchanged).


| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.
- Tuned for MI350X: 256×256×64 tiles, 8 warps, 2 stages for forward and dlhs; 256×128×64, 4 warps, 1 stage for drhs; plus chiplet-aware program order. Blackwell, TPU and megablox are unchanged.
- Per call on one GPU at batch 64 (M=131072), before → after TFLOP/s:

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

  A dense `jnp.matmul` of the same FLOPs runs at about 925–958; XLA fp16 `ragged_dot` at 24–98. At batch 8 the forward pass goes from 2.27 ms to 0.36 ms. Jobs 453500 and 453564.
- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

</details>

🤖 Matmul-alone time in the MI350X `--overlap` runs (jobs 453572, 453633, 453651) takes one of two values between runs: about 2.46 ms in `min64`, `ring`, `prio-on` and `lhs-prio-off`, and about 2.88 ms in the other 16. The faster overlap rows of `min64`, `ring` and `prio-on` (all-gather 5.68 ms against 6.05 ms in `base`) match that matmul gap, so they do not show an effect of the RCCL or XLA setting. Details: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9886#issuecomment-6047294744

Because the variance is between processes, re-timing the matmul inside a run does not remove it. To compare settings, run each setting in several processes, interleave them, and compare medians of a per-run ratio such as the hidden fraction `(t_collective + t_matmul − t_both) / min(t_collective, t_matmul)`, using the matmul-alone time of the same run.

### Token-deduplicated EP dispatch (`ring_dedup`): 1.580 s and 14.31% MFU with `save_moe`, -8.7% against ring

Commit: 91286fc (local; `ring_dedup` backend in b31085d, merged onto the gather-combine base 67ca557) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454021 (`ring_dedup`), 454012 (ring baseline)

PR: #9880 (draft, merge after #9860). `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` comes from #9852.

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.580 s | 165,900 | 14.31% | 206.5 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What it does.** `ring` all-gathers every token to all 8 GPUs and reduce-scatters a full-size output, but with top-4 of 256 experts a token reaches only 3.3 GPUs on average. `ring_dedup` (new module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring_dedup.py`) sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`, plus a small `all_to_all` of per-row combine weights and local expert ids. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, grouped layout and Triton `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32 and returns one row per token. All hidden-width movement is a gather (ring's `_dispatch_rows`/`_combine_rows`), so there are no scatter-adds in either pass.
- **Sender capacity** is `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing (0.416 × 32,768 per GPU). At 1.1 it sends 537 MB per collective per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring's all-gather or reduce-scatter (46%), and drops no tokens at the sender in these runs.
- **A/B, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile cache per job, `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, median of steps 2-19:**

  | Base | Remat | ring | `ring_dedup` | Jobs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | merged (gather combine + Triton routing top-k) | recompute_all | 1.798 s, 12.57% | 1.688 s, 13.40% (-6.1%) | 454022, 454026 |
  | merged | save_moe | 1.730 s, 13.07% | 1.580 s, 14.31% (-8.7%) | 454012, 454021 |
  | before the gather combine | recompute_all | 1.865 s, 12.13% | 1.735 s, 13.03% (-7.0%) | 453921, 453922 |
  | before the gather combine | save_moe | 1.842 s, 12.28% | 1.637 s, 13.81% (-11.1%) | 453960, 453968 |

  The two changes stack partly. With `save_moe`, the gather combine alone saves 112 ms, `ring_dedup` alone 205 ms, both together 262 ms. Peak memory changes by at most 0.7 GiB. Step-19 loss is within 8e-4 of ring in every pair. The drop rate is 1.00% vs 0.99% (`recompute_all`) and 1.12% vs 0.93% (`save_moe`).
- **Numerics.** f32 CPU unit tests on 8 shards match ring and a dense reference to 1e-5 in value and in gradients for x, combine weights and both expert weights, including a forced sender-drop case. At full shapes in bf16 on MI350X, one layer differs from ring by 0.2-0.5% relative in value and gradients. That comes from ring's bf16 summation; `ring_dedup` sums in f32.
- **Profile (steps 10-12, GPU 0, ms per profiled step, ring vs `ring_dedup`, both before the gather combine).** `recompute_all`: large EP collectives take 481 vs 311, exposed collective time is 357 vs 288, and MoE dispatch/combine kernels take 150 vs 42. `save_moe`: 386 vs 211, 402 vs 266, and 147 vs 40. Each large `all_to_all` takes 1.6-2.7 ms, against 3.3-4.2 ms for ring's collectives.
- **What is still exposed:** the forward return and backward dy `all_to_all`s are synchronous (about 60 ms each per step), and the small metadata `all_to_all`s take 0.8-0.9 ms per call under `save_moe`, where they queue behind the large transfers.
- The latency-hiding scheduler gave 1.594 s vs 1.637 s before the merge, but 1.591 s vs 1.580 s after it (job 454027), so leave it off.
- One run (454010) hit the step-5 GPU-7 out-of-memory on a 96.6 GiB allocation, the same failure seen at batch 96 in job 453660, and hung. The retry (454021) ran clean. Since diagnosed as allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer and fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- **Follow-ups:** packing the metadata into the activation rows and chunking the expert MLP were tried and did not help; see the next comment. Not tested on TPU or NVIDIA.

</details>

- Metadata in rows: the combine weights (f32 bits), local expert ids (int16) and the sender count ride in 16 extra bf16 columns of the dispatch all-to-all, and a custom VJP returns the combine-weight gradients in the backward dx all-to-all. One layer at batch-64 shapes gives bit-identical outputs and gradients against the current ring_dedup, with 4 all-to-alls instead of 6. The full model does not get faster: profiled steps drop 60 ms, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms per collective call, and the backward dx all-to-all becomes synchronous.
- Token chunks: each shard runs dispatch, expert MLP and return per token chunk. With the default GPU schedule, every all-to-all done follows its start with no GEMM in between, so nothing overlaps and chunking is 1.5-2.5% slower. With the latency-hiding scheduler, the transfers do overlap the other chunk's GEMMs, but half-size `ragged_dot` calls take 13% longer (332 -> 375 ms per profiled step), which cancels the gain. Without drops, chunked outputs and dx match exactly; per-chunk receiver capacity doubles receiver drops at capacity 1.0 (0.08% -> 0.15% in one layer). Not proposed.
- The latency-hiding scheduler now helps ring_dedup with recompute_all by about 2% (1.709 -> 1.668-1.678 s). save_moe without it is still fastest.
- Loss at step 19 matches base within 2e-4 in every run; drop rates are 1.0-1.2%.
- Two of 19 full-model runs hit the known step-3 single ~97 GiB allocation failure and hung; the retries ran clean. This is the allocator fragmentation fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` (#9901).
- Next: overlap the synchronous forward return and backward dy all-to-alls (about 55 ms each per profiled step) with work that does not shrink the GEMMs, such as the shared-expert MLP backward.

</details>

### One gradient all-reduce per weight after the layer scan: works, keeps gradients, no speedup on MI350X

Commit: bd8e11a · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Job: 453915 (on 60b253d), 454011 (on 67ca557)

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash --remat-mode <recompute_all|save_moe>
```

| Base | Remat | Variant | Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60b253d | recompute_all | baseline | 1.844 s | 142,200 | 12.26% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.852 s | 141,600 | 12.21% | 158.4 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | baseline | 1.824 s | 143,700 | 12.39% | 205.8 GiB |
| 60b253d | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.856 s | 141,200 | 12.18% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | baseline | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | recompute_all | deferred reduction | 1.786 s | 146,800 | 12.66% | 157.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | baseline | 1.748 s | 150,000 | 12.94% | 205.9 GiB |
| 67ca557 | save_moe | deferred reduction | 1.741 s | 150,600 | 12.99% | 205.9 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- What the in-scan all-reduces are: on this mesh (`expert=8`, other axes 1), every non-expert block weight is replicated across the batch. Explicit sharding types each layer's weight gradient as replicated, so the backward while body all-reduces it per layer. Per layer that is 5 gradient all-reduces: q/k/v/gate and w_o in the attention `cond` branch, one combined GatedNorm/router/shared w_gate/w_up, shared w_down, and the two RMSNorm weights. The forward body adds one router-stats all-reduce, for 6 × 26 = 156 per step. XLA's combiner can't merge across loop iterations or `cond` branches.
- The change: weights that only feed matmuls are marked `reduced` over the batch axes before the scan (`levanter.grug.sharding.defer_batch_grad_reduction`). Their gradients leave the scan unreduced and are all-reduced once per stacked weight. FSDP-sharded leaves (`data` > 1) are left unchanged. RMSNorm weights keep the per-layer reduction. Stored parameter shardings don't change.
- Gradients match. On CPU (tiny preset, f32, 8 devices) the loss and 26 of 27 leaves are bit-identical. On GPU (medium preset, bf16, job 454079) the loss is identical, and baseline-vs-change errors (at most 0.63% relative L2) equal baseline-vs-baseline. The full-model losses match too.
- The backward loop goes from 5 gradient all-reduces per layer to 1, but the step doesn't get faster. In a profiled A/B (job 453987) the change saves 43 ms per step, but the profiler adds about 0.3 ms to every collective call. Unprofiled, the 130 removed calls cost about 11 ms, and the single 2 GB all-reduce after the scan takes about 16 ms on the main stream. The bytes are the same either way, and the per-layer calls were bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound.
- Not proposing a PR for MI350X. Small collectives should be priced from unprofiled step times, not from trace durations.

</details>

### Hiding `ring_dedup`'s synchronous all-to-alls behind the shared expert: no gain

Commit: 3838b71 (local, on the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454847, 454872, 454943 (overlap + latency-hiding scheduler); 454865, 454945, 454949 (latency-hiding scheduler only); 454857, 454892 (baseline)

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton \
  XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

</details>
