## Grading concerns to resolve

The [Harbor verifier](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/e5a08396fce7bc230b2f023bbb568dbfa86b3ee8/adapters/scienceagentbench/template/tests/test.sh)
turns missing or unreadable evaluation results into zero rewards. Infrastructure
failures must remain distinguishable from valid model failures.

The verifier also copies gold references into the execution filesystem before
rerunning submitted code. Although they are hidden during agent generation, they
are accessible during that later execution. Separate submitted-program execution
from grading, including reference files and judge credentials. This is a static
boundary finding, not an observed exploitation result.

The upstream visual judge uses GPT-4o-2024-05-13, temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, 1,000 output
tokens, and three completions per request (`n=3`). Missing score markers become
zero in both inspected upstream and Harbor implementations. Decide and document
whether to preserve that behavior for parity or use an explicitly versioned
failure-aware protocol. Do not silently change grading semantics. Extract, pin, and test Verified's
exact task-success calculation, including aggregation across multiple figures
and mixed checks, pass thresholds, and missing candidate-output rules. Keep
malformed judge responses separate from valid negative judgments.

Sources: [upstream judge](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/gpt4_visual_judge.py),
[Harbor judge](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/e5a08396fce7bc230b2f023bbb568dbfa86b3ee8/adapters/scienceagentbench/llm_visual_judge.py).

## Execution route

The development pilot ran through the official EvalDash launcher with TaskSpec, Pi 0.87.0, and Daytona. TaskSpec describes the task, files, environment and grader. Pi runs the interactive coding session. A fresh sandbox replays the submitted program, then a separate grader receives its outputs and the publisher’s grading material. The shared-image task 66 record shows this path working end to end.

The initial plan followed BixBench’s Harbor adapter because the new-eval guide at the time covered non-agentic tasks. Harbor remains the comparison for the legacy ScienceAgentBench release, and BixBench provides the Pi and cohort settings. The native route now has a graded pilot in EvalDash. [Implementation PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11599) · [Historical non-agentic guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2dd5aa45254641ef3c2977afa49cdc2afa34c1e6/docs/tutorials/add-evaluation.md)

validity, CodeBERTScore, then cost to break ties. Its reported cost averages the
selected trajectories. Our operational cost report must count all attempts,
retries, and judge calls, including trajectories that were not selected.

The official [inference instructions](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/README.md#direct-prompting-and-self-debug)

defaults to `use_knowledge=False`. Including the supplied knowledge is a supported
benchmark variant. Here the repository agent means the authors' direct-prompting
and self-debug implementation, not a uniquely canonical agent protocol.
[Paper Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05080v3#S4.T3) reports both with-knowledge
and without-knowledge results for direct prompting, OpenHands CodeAct, and
self-debug. The code default does not establish a preferred paper setting.
These paper results predate Verified. Comparisons must match the knowledge
setting as well as the benchmark version. The selected plan is two separately
reported conditions for each of the three models: six model-condition cells.
One trial per task per model per knowledge condition is selected: 612 planned
solver trials, excluding validation and separately accounted infrastructure
retries. This protocol decision does not authorize execution or spending.

### Image preparation strategy (selected)

Selected: prepare and validate images before scored trials, then use immutable image digests
across models, knowledge conditions, and retries. This is compatible with the
TaskSpec image route, which requires resolving Docker build recipes before
execution. A fresh container per trial still preserves isolation; reusing an image
must never reuse a model's modified workspace.

BixBench and BFCL campaign configurations explicitly require preparing selected
task images with Pi before launch. Policy #10197 describes DS-1000 images built
from pinned Dockerfiles; that statement does not establish whether builds occur
for every trial or whether caches are reused. There is no single image-preparation
procedure established here for every policy evaluation.

A completed November 5 BixBench Pi run provides a narrower historical check:
its saved job configuration and 205-trial lock select the pinned Dockerfile-based
task repository, without a prepared-image override. A sampled trial completed
grading without an infrastructure exception. Those artifacts do not identify a
final prepared-image registry or digest, so they do not establish that the
current campaign's preparation requirement was followed in that run.

SAB's Harbor adapter provides Dockerfile recipes with scientific dependencies and
task input data. Those recipes can be built ahead of time. For the proposed
Verified implementation, invoke Pi only during the actor stage, keep clean replay
free of gold references and judge credentials, and expose private grading assets
only to the grading stage. Actor and replay use the same prepared scientific
environment; the replay stage runs the submitted Python program directly.

The pinned upstream container harness builds task dependencies from imports in
the submitted program using `pipreqs`, followed by task-specific installation
rules. It uses Python 3.10 and several version ranges rather than a complete lock.
That harness was released after the paper; it is not evidence of the paper's exact
environment. Fixed prepared images therefore change dependency provisioning.
Record the resolved package lock, system dependencies, base-image digests and recipe identity. Validate every reference program before scored use.

The shared software recipe pins the runtime across both knowledge conditions. Each fresh sandbox receives only the files for its task. Record disk use and staging time independently of solver time. A changed dependency requires a new recipe version and reference validation.

The image-build deadline governs preparation work, separately from the six-minute
agent setup, 60-minute solving, and 30-minute verifier budgets. Match BixBench's
preparation behavior without a benchmark-specific timeout override. Verify and
record the effective timeout in the preparation path before building; no explicit
campaign override does not imply unlimited build time. Harbor's 30-minute SAB
template allowance is comparison evidence, not the selected preparation limit.

### Timing evidence for the protocol decision

The [paper introduction](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05080v3#S1) says agents can
usually produce a meaningful program draft within 10 minutes. This is a broad
observation, not a reported end-to-end runtime distribution or agent deadline.
[Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05080v3#A1) says task collection was
restricted to programs that complete within 10 minutes; this concerns program
execution, not the entire agent session.

In upstream code at `c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d`,
[agent.py](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/agent.py)
allows up to 10 self-debug iterations and 900 seconds per program execution.
[run_eval.py](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/run_eval.py)
also uses 900 seconds for submitted-program execution. The
[Docker evaluation CLI](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench/blob/c26e151ed601ba109dc4d35e057ff8e73fec469d/evaluation/harness/run_evaluation.py)
defaults to 1,800 seconds for tests per instance. These are distinct limits.
The selected Pi agent budget is 60 minutes per task, matching the Harbor adapter
default. The selected verifier budget is 30 minutes total, including clean
execution capped at 900 seconds. These are Marin protocol choices, not
paper-specified agent deadlines.

| Choice | Alternative considered | Rationale and tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Official Verified release, preserving all 102 task IDs | Reuse the legacy Harbor dataset unchanged | Verified includes upstream corrections. It requires auditing updated artifacts and graders; legacy Harbor results remain historical comparisons, not Verified evidence. |
| Retain and flag the exposed answers in tasks 53 and 58 | Remove the three matching files for those tasks only | Keeping the published inputs preserves comparability. Removing them would create a corrected-input variant. |
| TaskSpec benchmark representation with Pi | Patch only the existing Harbor adapter, or use Marin's built-in ShellHarness | TaskSpec provides the target task contract; Pi matches the selected BixBench harness. A Harbor-only update could reuse more existing wiring, while TaskSpec plus Pi requires proving the shared runner integration. ShellHarness would change the selected agent. |
| One pinned modern harness: Pi 0.87.0 | Reproduce all three paper agent approaches or reuse Harbor's Claude Code parity harness | A single harness keeps the cohort comparison consistent with BixBench. This does not reproduce the paper's harness-dependent scores. |
| Separate knowledge-on and knowledge-off results | Choose only one condition or pool both | Both conditions are supported upstream. Separate reporting exposes the effect of supplied expert knowledge, at twice the solver workload of one condition. |
| One trial per task and condition | Paper-style per-task best of three, or Harbor-style repeated full runs | Matches the selected cohort protocol and limits execution cost. It provides less repeatability evidence than repeated runs and is not directly equivalent to best-of-three results. |
| Shared pinned software and per-task input staging | Bake each dataset into its own image, or install dependencies during solver time | The shared recipe allows both conditions to reuse the same software. Each task requires a separate transfer and checksum check before Pi starts. |
| Request 60-minute agent / 30-minute verifier limits | Adopt BixBench's 30-minute / 5-minute limits | Uses Harbor SAB's configured allowances for this scientific-programming workload. Longer limits increase potential cost and require an explicit policy revision; they are not yet an approved policy exception. |
| Qwen panel: 101 eligible tasks in each condition | A two-task model pilot before the full panel | The 202-trial panel measures benchmark-wide coverage, failures, runtime, and cost and can contribute directly to final results. It exposes more compute to integration failures, so full reference validation precedes it. |
| Official launcher, retained artifacts, and EvalDash | A standalone runner with manually reported scores | Follows the evidence path exemplified by SimpleQA Verified. It requires completing shared integration rather than treating standalone execution as an official result. |
| Preserve official inputs within the initial 10 GiB allocation | Reduce data or exclude oversized tasks | First remove redundant packaging and caches without changing task semantics. Input reductions or exclusions remain contingent alternatives requiring an explicitly identified variant or subset and revised counts. |

## Work plan and acceptance criteria

- [ ] Audit original and Verified artifact bundles, recording evaluator, reference,
  input-data, and dependency changes alongside annotation revisions and checksums.
- [ ] Complete the implementation checks below, resolve remaining protocol decisions,
  and record a frozen configuration.
- [ ] Implement population-preserving TaskSpec conversion for all 102 Verified tasks.
- [ ] Establish the supported interactive evaluation route, including clean program
  replay, separate grading, failure classification, and resource requirements.
- [ ] Use the official cohort launch workflow and its resource controls for
  preparation, validation, and the full Qwen panel. Record resolved allocations
  and cost accounting; escalate any requirements outside that workflow.
- [ ] Verify knowledge-off isolation across all actor-visible inputs and test
  the pinned task-success aggregation, thresholds, and missing-output rules.
- [ ] Validate all oracles and representative negative controls through the supported
  validation workflow; investigate stochastic failures and reference isolation
  without silently changing thresholds. Reference-solution validation for all
  102 Verified tasks is a required gate before the Qwen panel; unresolved
  reference failures must be resolved or receive an explicit protocol decision.
- [ ] Run the full official-path panel with the cohort's `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`,
  using its frozen cohort revision and settings: 101 eligible Verified tasks in each of the two
  knowledge conditions, 202 logical solver trials total, selected. Validate the
  official launcher, retained evidence, and EvalDash. Check displayed coverage
  and grades against raw archives, and separately exercise infrastructure-failure
  handling. These results count toward the final 612-trial cohort panel if the
  frozen protocol remains unchanged and reporting gates are met; no duplicate
  Qwen run is required. Review Qwen outcomes before proceeding to GPT-OSS and
  Gemma. Execution remains contingent on implementation and validation readiness.
- [ ] Complete full runs for the selected cohort models under frozen settings.
  Link EvalDash runs and durable evidence; report coverage, uncertainty, failure
  counts, runtime, accelerator/sandbox use, judge costs, and retry accounting.
  Retain all 102 task IDs and report planned trials, attempted trials, validly
  graded trials, and successes; retain ungraded outcomes separately.
- [ ] Audit grading and compare with upstream Verified or an explicitly matched
  reference protocol. Keep legacy results and protocol deviations separately labeled.
- [ ] Present the ID-admission recommendation: measured scientific-programming
  capabilities, paired model outcomes, grading reliability, reproducibility,
  operational cost, and limitations. No incremental-coverage or overlap study
  against BixBench/DS-1000 is required.

Completion requires a reviewable evidence package and an explicit admission
recommendation. Implementation or dashboard registration alone does not satisfy
this issue. A small model panel provides initial comparative evidence, not a
robust correlation study.

## Implementation checks and remaining approvals

The protocol choices above are selected. The following are implementation work
and review dependencies, rather than prerequisites for filing this proposal.

### Implementation checks

- Resolve and freeze the existing cohort revisions for Qwen, GPT-OSS, and Gemma.
- Verify and freeze BixBench's effective network policy, including inherited
  task/backend settings, for reuse across both knowledge conditions. Document
  benchmark-specific download requirements; any deviation needs an explicit
  protocol decision.
- Verify BixBench's effective preparation timeout and reuse its behavior without
  a benchmark-specific override. With the infrastructure retry
  limit fixed at 10 and backoff fixed at multiplier 2 / 1–60 seconds, finalize applicable
  error categories and stage-specific
  recovery behavior without rerunning successfully completed stages unnecessarily.
- Confirm whether 10 GiB is a required disk ceiling or a campaign allocation.
  If a Verified task exceeds the adopted ceiling, first remove redundant caches
  and packaging overhead without changing task inputs or grading. Reducing data
  or excluding tasks requires an explicit protocol decision and a separately
  identified modified variant or subset, with an exclusion manifest and revised
  task counts. Such exclusions are not infrastructure missingness under the
  90% reporting gate; the full 102-task protocol remains the target meanwhile.
- Use the selected MiniMax visual judge with three independent calls per comparison. The completed controls and routing deviation are recorded below. Agreement with the upstream GPT-4o judge remains unmeasured.

### Remaining protocol and ownership decisions

- Agree on comparison evidence required for externally reported scores. The
  selected reporting gate is ≥90% valid scored coverage per model/knowledge
  condition; preserve all 102 task IDs and apply the policy uncertainty adjustment.
- Who owns the shared agentic evaluation-runner changes and policy admission review?
- Obtain policy-owner approval of the requested ScienceAgentBench Verified
  revision permitting 60-minute agent / 30-minute verifier limits. Requesting
  this revision is selected; approval remains outstanding against the existing
  30-minute / 5-minute limits.

## Official path and current state

The task 66 pilot used the native TaskSpec path through the official launcher. The remaining full-panel work includes reference validation and grading recovery. [Launcher documentation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/246f795749166285a864e891e56facfbcf9127e7/experiments/evaluation/README.md) · [Implementation PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11599)

### Visual-judge decision (November 17)

Marin uses the BixBench MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 checkpoint with vision enabled. Each
comparison sends the candidate plot first and the gold plot second, with the
original prompt, temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, and a 1,000-token output limit.
Average three separate single-completion requests. A response without a matching
score marker contributes zero. A failed call or missing completion leaves the
comparison ungraded.

Both the model substitution and the change from one three-completion request
are deviations from upstream. In a six-call synthetic control, MiniMax scored
identical charts 100/100/100 and a reversed data trend 25/25/25. This checks
image-pair handling and basic discrimination at task 66’s threshold of 60.
Agreement with the upstream judge has not been measured.

Task 66’s saved reference-program plot received three scores of 100/100 from the Marin-hosted MiniMax judge. The pinned task evaluator returned reward 1 at its threshold of 60. This checks the saved reference output. Task 92 separately passed through the Harbor verifier. At that checkpoint, official Qwen solver starts and grades were 0/204.

### Shared environments and paired corpus, November 19

The curated pipeline built and reloaded all **204 rows** across the two knowledge conditions. Each condition has 102 task IDs, 64 visual evaluators and 38 deterministic evaluators. Expert knowledge changes the prompt for 98 tasks. Four tasks have identical prompts in both conditions. These are corpus counts. The 64 visual tasks contain 65 figure comparisons. Three judge calls per comparison imply up to 390 candidate calls across both knowledge conditions. Visual reference validation would add up to 195 calls, approved under the same aggregate $5 ceiling. The full 2-CPU, 8-GiB Qwen panel has 0/204 graded trials. Official pilot evidence covers one distinct task/condition. The initial implementation and the shared-software validation both scored 0 on task 66, knowledge off. Treat them as two integration runs on the same case.

| Check | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Actor and clean replay | Fresh sandboxes reuse a pinned Pi/scientific software snapshot. The runner stages each task’s selected files after startup. The 405 selected files across 71 directories match the published release digests. Tasks 53 and 58 keep the documented answer-file exposures in both conditions. |
| Largest input | Three files totaling 905,216,384 bytes passed in-sandbox SHA-256 checks in 138.2 seconds with 10 GiB disk. A prior range-based attempt lost its publisher connection. Fetching the pinned archive once and extracting on the runner succeeded. |
| Offline plotting | Some climate references call Cartopy for a public coastline or land layer. The runner stages the same checksummed Natural Earth files before actor and replay startup for tasks 48, 49, 56 and 86 in both knowledge conditions. Their sandboxes keep network access disabled. Native clean replay produced all six tested plots (48, 49, 55, 56, 66 and 86), and task 66 still matched its previously graded reference output byte for byte. |
| Private grading inputs | The corpus identifies the 102 published evaluators and required gold members by path, size and checksum. The task 66 software-only grader started empty and passed both its evaluator and target-figure checksums after staging. No judge call was needed for this check. |
| Shared scientific dependencies | Tasks 29, 34, 35 and 92 also passed the native clean-replay and separate-grader path with replay exit 0 and reward 1 each. Task 66 reproduced its previously graded plot byte for byte. Adding the missing runtime library let task 32 produce its figure. Output creation alone provides no visual grade. |
| CPU and memory | Native Daytona defaults gave these reference sandboxes 1 GiB of RAM. Tasks 14, 21 and 23 each exited 137 with a recorded out-of-memory kill. The completed BixBench comparison trial requested 2 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM through its [pinned task](https://github.com/penfever/harbor-datasets/blob/454d04b5427fd90de78d7bec9dfe57561a21ff03/datasets/bixbench-cli-marin-corrections-1/bix-1-q1/task.toml), and the campaign set disk to 10 GiB. With those BixBench requests, all three references finished with no out-of-memory kills. Task 21 received reward 1. Tasks 14 and 23 produced plots. Their peak memory ranged from 1.07 to 1.45 GiB. The full-panel recipe now requests 2 CPUs, 8 GiB RAM and 10 GiB disk explicitly. |

At the November 19 checkpoint, CPU diagnostics had exercised 73 of the 102 publisher reference programs across shared-image revisions. Nineteen distinct deterministic references received reward 1, including ten through native clean replay and a separate grader (16, 18, 19, 21, 29, 34, 35, 40, 53 and 92). Task 41’s publisher program exited successfully twice and received reward 0 both times. The released evaluator (eval_MD_KNN.py) sets the mean F1 threshold at 0.73 across three prediction files. Our measured mean F1 was 0.70433. The Verified annotation credits Anika Liu and coauthors’ [CAMDA-DILI source study](https://github.com/anikaliu/CAMDA-DILI). Its linked models_MD.py uses random forests and SVMs. The benchmark authors distributed the KNN adaptation (MD_KNN.py) and its scorer in their [Verified release](https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench#updates). The original study pinned scikit-learn 0.21.2 and Python 3.6.7. The benchmark harness installs scikit-learn without an exact version. The shared image uses scikit-learn 1.7.2. Separate replays with scikit-learn 1.5.2 and 1.4.2 produced the same mean F1 as 1.7.2, to all recorded digits. These checks leave the origin of the 0.73 threshold unresolved. Task 90 received zero because its reference failed during clean replay with the 900-second limit. Its saved diagnostic omits the exit reason, so timeout attribution is unconfirmed. Tasks 21 and 53 encountered network failures on two native grading attempts each. Both recovered after adding a fallback from interrupted range reads to the full digest-verified release. Their publisher references passed native grading with reward 1. Task 53 retains its documented answer exposure. All of these are environment and scoring controls, separate from Qwen results.

The 29 references still unattempted at that checkpoint included three glacier tasks that import OGGM (64, 65 and 74), two materials tasks that import MODNet (101 and 102), and two EEG tasks that import PyTorch (71 and 72). The new image includes CPU PyTorch. These import checks identify the next validation work. They do not establish that any reference runs successfully.

Three additional references identified gaps in the shared dependency lock. Task 30 expects an older Phonopy API, task 36 requires a BioPsyKit release with MuseDataset, and task 69 requires scikit-misc. The BioPsyKit versions exposing MuseDataset depend transitively on docopt, which has no compatible wheel on the selected index. A lock pinning docopt 0.6.2 built successfully in a single private image with BioPsyKit 0.11.0, Phonopy 2.38.2, scikit-misc 0.5.3 and the CPU-only PyTorch wheel. The new private shared image produced the expected plots for tasks 30 and 36. Fourteen additional references finished, including a deterministic pass on task 44 and output plots on the other thirteen. Task 69 progressed to execution but exceeded the short 180-second diagnostic allowance. With the configured 900-second allowance, native clean replay finished successfully on task 69 and produced its 97,885-byte plot. Task 66’s reference plot remained byte-identical after the image change. Neither replay called a judge.

Two initial official staged-input attempts failed during Daytona startup. A subsequent snapshot-backed attempt was preempted and hit its single-attempt cap on recovery. Its archive contained a start record and no completed response or grade. At that checkpoint, reference controls were pending for the original 204-trial plan. The [official shared-software task 66 run](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20261119-194500-qwen3.6-35b-a3b-9d050394062043259c60bdafbc0db1dd-scienceagentbench-verified-66-knowledge-off-08d3fc592fd85680ac9670b7ab000efe) finished successfully. Clean replay exited 0. The three visual grades were 45, 30 and 55, for a mean of 43.33 against the task threshold of 60 and a binary reward of 0. The run used 34,368 prompt tokens and 2,459 completion tokens. The three judge calls cost $0.00314458 in total. It used the earlier 1 GiB pilot allocation.

The pilot capped each trial at one attempt. The native runner checks its attempt cap on resume, and skips completed grades, submission failures and invalid tasks. For agent episodes it can rerun the solver after a grading infrastructure failure. The full-panel launch needs an explicit mapping for the selected ten infrastructure retries, recovery of saved submissions where possible, and accounting that enforces the aggregate judge budget across retries.

On November 19, the approved OpenRouter/DeepInfra FP8 reference check on task 66 scored 100 in all three completions. The publisher reference passed its threshold of 60 at a cost of $0.001097144. This is a reference control. The official Qwen candidate grade remains 0/1.

On November 20, visual reference replay covered all 64 visual tasks. Fifty-three produced plots and eleven failed before judging (9, 17, 38, 39, 52, 64, 65, 70, 74, 75, 98). The Qwen panel has no separate wall-clock cutoff. Per-task limits and the aggregate visual-judge budget still apply.

🤖 The [Nov 21 SkyRL nightly](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/44925403052/job/136910257408) reached the Grug GPU suite: 33 tests passed, then `test_grug_megatron_eval_forward_is_independent_of_peer_rank_batch[toy_top4-pp1_ep2]` failed during Megatron optimizer initialization. The native traceback ends at `torch.distributed.all_gather_object` with NCCL `invalid usage`: “No algorithm/protocol nor symKernelId available for function AllGather ... NCCL_ALGO was set to allreduce:tree.” OPD and CatCount passed; this was a test/runtime failure after placement, not a cluster admission failure.

The repository's [batch-invariant worker settings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/batch_invariant.py#L12-L23) set `NCCL_ALGO=allreduce:tree`, and [Ray propagates that setting to the learner](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/utils.py#L511-L514). [NCCL's syntax](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html#nccl-algo) requires a default algorithm for functions outside a function-specific override. This setting leaves `AllGather` without one.

I’ll update the setting to permit Ring for other collectives while retaining Tree for all-reduce, then run the failing GPU case and the repository checks before opening a fix PR.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body: Forwarding servers don't serve any queries, so the index building and remote object backups are unnecessary. They should simply collect and forward logs from their locally compacted segments.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Locate Finelog forwarding-server code and index/backup logic
- [x] Determine root cause and scope
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PR; #8748 is adjacent object-storage work)
- [x] Post analysis — **out of PR scope: design change, needs human review**

---

**Research**

Forwarding servers are ordinary `Live` stores that additionally spawn a `Forwarder`; the store itself has no notion of a forwarding-only role, so per-namespace maintenance runs the full `flush → compact → sync → evict → index-backfill` cycle regardless ([`run_maintenance`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L1934-L2015)). Index building is gated only by the static per-namespace policy [`segment_indexes_enabled_for`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/policies.rs#L164-L167), which is identical on hub and regional servers — there is no server-role input to turn it off for a forwarder. Remote backup is [`sync_step`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L1512), uploading L≥1 segments to the object store.

The blocker is that remote backup is load-bearing for **retention**, not just durability. Eviction reclaims only `BOTH` (local+remote) segments via `select_eviction_candidate`, and [`evict_segment`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L1644-L1679) refuses to destroy `LOCAL`-only data — the test `eviction_skips_local_only_when_no_remote` (namespace.rs:3987) asserts local-only segments are never evicted. So dropping backup on a forwarder as configured today grows local disk without bound; there is no size/age reclamation path for local-only segments.

**Proposed approach (for review — not implementing as a PR)**

Doing this safely is three coupled changes, not a two-line gate, so it exceeds the self-contained-bugfix bar:

1. **Server-role signal.** Thread a forwarding-only flag from the CLI (`args.forwarding` non-empty, already parsed in [main.rs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/main.rs#L303)) through `Store::new*` into each `Namespace`, rather than deriving indexing from the global static policy. Decide whether this is a new `ServeMode` variant (`Forward`) or an orthogonal boolean — `ServeMode` currently means "what a process may touch," and forward-only fits that framing.
2. **Gate the two steps.** Skip `sync_step` and index backfill in `run_maintenance` when forwarding-only (leaving `cleanup_disabled_index_bundles` to remove stale bundles on a converted server).
3. **Retention for local-only segments.** Since the hub becomes the durable archive for forwarded rows, a forwarding-only store must treat local segments as ephemeral scratch and evict `LOCAL`-only segments by size/age. This is a new eviction path; the forwarder is already best-effort and tolerates eviction removing un-forwarded segments ([forwarding.rs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/forwarding.rs#L27-L44)), so at-least-once semantics hold, but the "evict rows that never forwarded" behavior is a policy decision worth an explicit sign-off.

Open questions for a maintainer: (a) is a forwarding server ever queried locally as a fallback (the forwarder docstring calls the local store "the system of record")? If yes, dropping indexes/backup changes that guarantee. (b) Should local-only eviction wait on the forward cursor, or stay purely size/age-bounded? Deploy wiring in [`config.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/config.py#L219-L241) (forwarders currently also set `remote_log_dir`) would follow whichever shape is chosen.

issues.body:
The November 21 two-slice `v6e-8` smoke exceeded the 135-minute Actions wait while its Iris training child was still running. At 20:01 UTC, Iris reported 0/2 tasks complete, four failures, and five worker preemptions. Repeated worker RPC loss interrupted JAX compilation; the reason the workers stopped accepting RPCs is unknown.

Reproduce:
1. At revision `cb991a5a5c8a`, run `python -m experiments.ferries.grug_multislice_smoke` through Iris with two `v6e-8` slices in `us-east5` and five steps.
2. Inspect this run's two training tasks and their attempts. The first slice-1 worker stopped accepting Reconcile RPCs at 18:22:19 UTC; Iris marked it failed at 18:23:16. JAX on task 0 then aborted after task 1 stopped sending heartbeats. Further worker losses caused retries through the Actions timeout.

Expected: both workers remain reachable through compilation and the smoke completes five steps within the CI wait.

<details><summary>Evidence and scope</summary>

- Finelog `marin` / `log`: controller key `/system/controller`, seq `31893221673` (connection refused) and `31893243836` (worker failed). Task key `/runner/iris-run-job-20261121-174344/grug-train-grug-multislice-smoke-44931566955-1/0:0`, seq `31893235259–31893235267` (JAX reports task 1 heartbeat loss and aborts). Worker loss recurred at controller seq `31893757969` and `31894782491`.
- Finelog `marin` / `iris.task`, 17:40–20:10 UTC: task 0 had five attempts and task 1 had six. Their peak process memory samples were 50,442 MiB and 50,903 MiB on the first attempts; the task request was 386.55 GB per slice. These samples do not establish host health.

The worker's process logs show Docker profile probes failing before the first RPC loss, but do not identify why its RPC endpoint became unreachable.

</details>

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
SkyRL RL rollouts have about a dozen independent limits on how much work generates at once. Several have coupled defaults, so changing one knob silently moves another, and the engine throughput of a run depends on whichever one binds first. In the Mochi throughput sprint (#11954) the binding limit changed three times as we raised knobs one at a time, and each change needed a code read to explain.

Limits on the rollout path (paths relative to `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/`, read at `3a859712f5` on `benfeuer/long-loop-prototype`; the same code is on `main`):

| Layer | Knob | What it caps |
|---|---|---|
| Buffer (`rollouts/buffer.py`) | `trainer.rollout_buffer.max_in_flight` | Prompt groups generating at once, across all routes. When null, an Iris launch derives it as 1.5 batches, capped at Harbor `n_concurrent_trials / n_samples_per_prompt` (`config/ppo_base_config.yaml:248-251`), so 256 / 8 = 32. |
| Buffer | `max_staleness_steps` with `batch_policy: full_batch` | How many batches generation may lease ahead of training (`FullBatchRolloutPolicy.lease_batch`). This binds during step 1, because the step waits for its slowest group. |
| Buffer | `consumed_route_quotas` | Agentic and nonagentic groups per batch. `experiments/post_training/long_loop/nvl72.py` overwrote an explicit `{}` with `batch_size // 2` each until `30d6357c55`. |
| Worker pool (`rollouts/workers.py`) | `trajectory_runner.rollout_workers.num_workers`, `cpus_per_worker` | Not a cap by itself, because workers are async actors. It divides the Harbor cap into per-worker shares, and `num_workers * cpus_per_worker` must fit the driver node's CPUs. |
| Task worker (`rollouts/task_worker.py:390-395, 763`) | `trajectory_runner.max_concurrent_tasks` | Trajectories per worker (1,024 by default). |
| Task worker | `terminal_bench.harbor.n_concurrent_trials // num_workers` | Harbor-routed trajectories per worker, held for the whole trial. The pool dispatches groups to the least-loaded worker with no regard to free Harbor slots (`workers.py:271-275`). |
| Task worker | `rollout_workers.executor_threads`, `task_sessions.max_verifier_workers` | Blocking-operation and verifier threads per worker (256 and 32 by default). |
| Graders | `_SYMBOLIC_SLOTS = BoundedSemaphore(8)` (`skyrl-gym/.../math_with_judge.py:62`), GenRM `max_concurrent_comparisons`, teacher-oracle capacity | Grading throughput for specific sources. |
| External | Daytona org quota and create rate, remote judge rate limits, vLLM `max_num_seqs` / `gpu_memory_utilization` / `max_num_batched_tokens` | Sandboxes, judge calls, and engine slots. |

Observed effect, all on Mochi on cw-us-east-08a with 12 rollout GB200 GPUs:
- The baseline (`max_in_flight` 32, the derived default) ran at about 56 generated tok/s per GPU.
- Raising `max_in_flight` to 128 doubled that for about 25 minutes, then it fell to 34 tok/s per GPU when the staleness lookahead ran out.
- Raising staleness let the engines fill up (30 of 32 sequences running per engine). At that point vLLM capacity became the limit.

Each of these needed a separate code trace to explain.

Done when: the rollout path has one documented concurrency budget, from which the per-resource limits (Harbor sandboxes, judge calls, verifier threads) are derived or explicitly declared. A run logs, at startup, the effective value of every limit in the table. At runtime, it logs which limit blocked admission.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

At `cb991a5` on main, the buffer returns `None` for both its group cap and the batch-policy lease window; `acquire_lease` then waits without retaining the cause. Task and Harbor semaphores queue work after dispatch, while the pool chooses the worker with the fewest pending calls, regardless of free Harbor slots. The current main schema uses `groups_per_family`; the long-loop branch's `consumed_route_quotas` needs reconciliation when that branch adopts this change. No open PR claims #11957; [#10501](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10501) changes worker placement and should be checked during implementation.

**Relevant code**
- [`buffer.py#L563-L577`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/buffer.py#L563-L577): group-cap wait loses its cause.
- [`buffer.py#L469-L485`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/buffer.py#L469-L485): full-batch staleness window.
- [`task_worker.py#L379-L395`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_worker.py#L379-L395): worker-local caps.
- [`workers.py#L257-L288`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/workers.py#L257-L288): pending-count routing.
- [`sections.py#L438-L461`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/lib/skyrlrecipe/src/skyrlrecipe/sections.py#L438-L461): current recipe fields.

# Rollout concurrency budget

## Design

1. Add one typed budget to the SkyRL recipe: an explicit prompt-group cap and declared caps for Harbor trials, task execution, verifier threads, graders, and externally configured services. Give every entry a unit and scope. Resolve it once at launch and pass the resolved values to the buffer, worker pool, task workers, and graders; remove their independent launch-time defaults. Keep `max_staleness_steps` and `groups_per_family` as batch-policy settings, but include their effective admission ceilings in the same startup report. Record the configured value, effective value, and source for every limit in the issue's table, including worker CPU reservations and vLLM settings.
2. Partition global Harbor capacity among workers without exceeding the declared total, including non-divisible totals. Make Harbor-route dispatch aware of free worker slots so groups do not accumulate behind one worker while another can run them. Reject configurations that require positive Harbor slots on more workers than the global cap allows.
3. Have buffer admission return a typed block reason for group cap, unpublished policy, staleness window, or family quota. Measure waits at task, Harbor, verifier, and grader gates with stable reason names. Emit counters and wait durations when a gate blocks; avoid a log line for every poll. Use the existing [rollout wait telemetry](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollout_observability.py#L173-L183). Report external queueing or rate-limit responses separately when a provider does not expose its internal occupancy.
4. Document the budget's units, derivations, and precedence. Update all SkyRL recipe and long-loop call sites to the new schema.

## Costs / Risks

A group may spawn several trajectories, and only some use Harbor or a judge, so a single group count cannot stand in for resource occupancy. Capacity-aware routing changes worker fairness; compare route mix and throughput with the current scheduler, and reconcile #10501 before landing.

## Testing

Use deterministic buffer and worker tests for group-cap versus staleness blocking, mixed route quotas, non-divisible Harbor shares, worker saturation, and verifier/grader waits. Assert that the startup snapshot covers every listed limit and that each simulated block produces the matching reason and duration. Run the repository's package tests, type check, lint, and agentic lint review before a PR; validate one controlled rollout against the startup report and wait counters before treating throughput changes as measured.

## Open question

Daytona, remote judges, and vLLM may not expose a precise admission decision to SkyRL. I propose marking their internal occupancy as unknown in the startup report and logging observed queueing or rate-limit responses under an external-capacity reason.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Which limit bound in each Mochi arm (cw-us-east-08a, measured; full arm table and receipts in #11954):

| Run | Config (changed limit) | What bound | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| .103 baseline | `max_in_flight` 32 (derived default), 12 rollout GPUs | `max_in_flight` | 11.7/16 running per engine, about 56 tok/s per GPU |
| A1 | `max_in_flight` 128, staleness 3 | staleness lookahead (`full_batch`, 4 batches of 32) once fast groups committed | 113 tok/s per GPU in the first 25 min, then 34; running fell to 7/16 |
| A3 | seqs32, HBM 0.85, staleness 11 | vLLM engine slots | 30.5/32 running plus 5.9 waiting per engine, 430 pending requests; coordinator at 0.5% of one core (no GIL limit) |
| A5 | Harbor 384 | engine slots, plus long-context prefill (93% of tokens are prompt, prefix hit 20%, 66 preemptions) | prefill 1,663 tok/s per GPU vs decode 125 |
| A7 / A10 | expert parallel 16, seqs64 | client demand: engines underfilled | prefix hit 89-90%, 0 preemptions, 20-26/64 running, almost no queue |
| `.115` training (`5957d8bbcf`) | every pure cap raised; Harbor 384 (12 per worker); staleness 3; route quotas 16/16 | **buffer `batch_lookahead`** (128 groups leased) from 3:05 PM EST, and **Harbor slots** | 322 Harbor-slot waits with mean wait about 21 min; `max_in_flight` 1024, task slots, executor and verifier threads never logged as blocking; running fell from 31 to 18 of 64 per engine while step 1 waited for its slowest agentic group; 95 -> 66 tok/s per GPU |

What we learned from this:
- The binding limit moved four times as we raised knobs one at a time.
- After every pure semaphore was raised, two limits remained:
  - the staleness lookahead, a training-semantics choice;
  - Harbor's per-worker slot share, a real shared-Daytona resource.
- Both are aggravated by `full_batch` waiting for the slowest agentic group.
- The startup and blocked-cause logs that `cf7e04df26` adds on `benfeuer/long-loop-prototype` (`rollout_concurrency_configuration`, buffer blocker transitions, per-worker Harbor and task-slot wait/resume events) are what made this measurable. They are the logging this issue asks for.

issues.author: dbuddha
issues.body:
Hi all, I'm Deepak, a Stanford student, and I've been working on this as my CS221 project. It started from Will's suggestion to begin with the Delphi seed repeats, and from his note in the Nov 2 standup (#11169) that, with loop variance this high, it would help to have documented expected variance so agents know what counts as a regression. Calvin also suggested in #data-mixing that we target fewer evals, possibly one that generalizes well, instead of a big aggregate, so I tested one version of that too. Everything here uses public data, and I'm happy to share more detail on any of it.

## Short version

I measured how much eval scores move between training seeds of the same recipe. I used DataDecide's per-question results (3 seeds per recipe), and the public Delphi seed triples at 1e21 and 1e22, which I scored with Marin's eval suite and the pinned stanford-crfm harness.

The part I think is most useful for Marin is that item-sampling SE is not a good stand-in for seed noise, and it misses in both directions. For soft metrics like gold log-prob or BPB, item SE usually understates seed noise, sometimes several times over. For accuracy it depends on the task: item SE overstates seed noise for HellaSwag and MMLU on DataDecide, but understates it for Delphi MMLU 0-shot and for the DataDecide 10-task average. The ratio also moves with scale. For MMLU 0-shot log-prob on Delphi, seed SD is about 4x the item SE at 1e21 but about 1x at 1e22.

On Calvin's suggestion, picking a single eval by SNR went badly. The 10-task average picked the 1B winner in 82% of recipe pairs, and the highest-SNR single eval got 57%. The best single eval in hindsight did tie the average, so one eval can work if it's chosen for agreement with the target.

I also tried to forecast seed noise as a power law in compute, and that did not work.

## Why this matters for the current gates

Several gates set thresholds from item SEs or fixed bands, and the ones that use seed replicates have only a few:

- The release tie rule in #10197 uses unpaired item SEs. There is an open question there about paired SEs. For picking one fixed release checkpoint, item SE may be the right noise. Seed noise matters when the call is about a recipe.
- Data Belay (#11582) uses 3 seeds per arm with a 1% floor, and suggests pooling the control's seed variance across rungs.
- The loop presets in #10740 compare against a few control replicates.
- #11177 notes that paired-item variance is unmeasured.
- #10804 notes that interval calibration for Micro210 is not established.
- Belay (#9451) uses a fixed 0.005 band.
- Ladder forecasts like #10753 fit one run per rung, so seed noise at the small rungs goes straight into the extrapolation.

#5247 is the closest earlier work on choosing a useful set of evals. It measured noise from 10 repeat runs at 300M and ended on using the smooth proxy with the highest SNR, which is the rule Result 2 tests.

## What I measured

**DataDecide** (`allenai/DataDecide-eval-instances`, revision `23f3b2e`). 10 OLMES tasks, using each task's primary metric and the gold-choice log-prob per character. I used two subsets:

- Eval selection (Results 2 and 3): 24 of the 25 recipes, 3 seeds each, read at the last step that every recipe and seed shares: 150M at 37,500, 300M at 45,000 and 1B at 69,369. These are about 98% of training for the two smaller sizes, and final for 1B. I left out `dolma1.7-no-math-no-code`, because its 1B seed 4 only has a checkpoint at 57,500.
- Noise forecast and the DataDecide ratios (Results 1 and 4): 5 recipes (`c4`, `dclm-baseline`, `dolma1.7`, `falcon-with-cc`, `fineweb-edu`) at all five sizes, each read at the last step its three seeds share. For 530M and 750M that step is at 89% and 43% of the schedule.

**Delphi on Marin's suite.**

- Checkpoints: `delphi-1e21-3.4Bparams-46.3Btokens` and `delphi-1e22-9.7Bparams-160Btokens`, default seed plus seeds 42 and 62746.
- Tasks: `mmlu_sl_verb` 0-shot and 5-shot, and the `logprob_gsm8k_5shot` and `logprob_humaneval_10shot` configs from [`experiments/exp1337_eval_suite.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f08afdb5ec98c742c06a5e72d9a987aa9db1e450/experiments/exp1337_eval_suite.py) (since removed from main in #6633).
- Harness: `stanford-crfm/lm-evaluation-harness@d5e3391f` with the HF backend on one H100, BF16 weights, batch size auto. I logged per-sample results.
- I recreated the two logprob tasks as YAML with the same fields as the suite. I computed BPB per document from the logged log-likelihood and the target's bytes.

**Delphi GSM8K rollouts.** The per-seed rollouts that `tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws` (commit `c0490e5`) published: 256 problems for every seeded Delphi budget, with 32 rollouts per hint level and 64 unhinted. That repo has no license file, so I only report aggregates from it.

## Results

### 1. Seed noise vs item SE on Delphi

Each value is seed SD divided by item SE. Seed SD is taken across the three seeds, and item SE comes from the default seed (micro averages).

| Metric | 1e21 | 1e22 |
|---|---:|---:|
| MMLU 0-shot accuracy | 1.28 | 1.35 |
| MMLU 0-shot gold-choice log-prob | 4.10 | 1.03 |
| MMLU 5-shot accuracy | 0.71 | 0.69 |
| MMLU 5-shot gold-choice log-prob | 1.99 | 1.83 |
| GSM8K 5-shot BPB | 2.61 | 0.56 |
| HumanEval 10-shot BPB (see the fidelity note) | 0.05 | 1.02 |

DataDecide (the 5-recipe subset) shows a similar split. For accuracy on HellaSwag and MMLU, seed SD is 0.3x to 0.75x the item SE, but for BoolQ accuracy it is 4x to 9x. For gold log-prob on ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and MMLU it is 1.1x to 12x, and it is largest at 530M and 750M, whose checkpoints come before the end of the LR schedule. Across all 10 tasks, gold log-prob ranges from 0.3x (WinoGrande) to 88x (BoolQ).

So I don't think one rule of thumb works. An item-SE tie rule is on the cautious side for some accuracy metrics, too willing to call differences real for others, and too willing for most soft metrics. These ratios are exploratory, not part of a preregistered test.

### 2. Does one eval recover the winner? (Calvin's suggestion)

Setup: I picked a recipe using results at 300M (or 150M), and counted it correct if it matched the sign of the 3-seed mean macro accuracy at 1B, over all 276 recipe pairs. SNR is the spread of recipe means divided by the pooled seed SD, measured at 150M only. I wrote the plan down before computing any of these numbers.

| Decide at | Seeds per recipe | 10-task average | Highest-SNR single eval (HellaSwag gold log-prob) | Best single eval in hindsight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 300M | 1 | 0.822 | 0.570 | CSQA accuracy, 0.819 |
| 300M | 3 | 0.848 | 0.569 | CSQA accuracy, 0.848 |
| 150M | 1 | 0.797 | 0.600 | OpenBookQA gold log-prob, 0.786 |
| 150M | 3 | 0.808 | 0.605 | CSQA accuracy, 0.815 |

At 300M with one seed per recipe, the bootstrap 95% interval for "single eval minus average" is -0.447 to -0.048. The interval resamples recipes, 2,000 draws. PIQA accuracy actually points the wrong way (0.44).

HellaSwag gold log-prob separates recipes very consistently, but in a different order from the broad target. Every eval here runs on the same training runs, so the average adds eval compute but no extra runs. My read is that fewer evals can work, as Calvin suggested, but the eval has to be chosen for agreement with the target, and low noise alone isn't enough. CSQA accuracy tied the average here, but I only know that in hindsight.

One fair objection is that the 1B target is accuracy, which is noisy. So I also scored the same 300M picks (one seed per recipe) against smooth 1B targets. This check is exploratory:

| Picked at 300M | 1B average accuracy (target above) | 1B average gold log-prob | 1B HellaSwag gold log-prob |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| HellaSwag gold log-prob (highest SNR) | 0.570 | 0.510 | 0.941 |
| Average of the 10 gold log-probs | 0.844 | 0.844 | 0.466 |
| Average of the 10 accuracies | 0.822 | 0.779 | 0.435 |

The two broad 1B targets agree on 90% of pairs, and the smooth one doesn't rescue the single eval. HellaSwag gold log-prob tracks HellaSwag itself across scale (94%), so the problem looks like breadth, not smoothness. Averaging the smooth proxies did best for both broad targets.

### 3. Tie rules on the aggregate

Decisions at 300M with one seed per recipe, on the 10-task average:

| Rule | Share of pairs it calls | Accuracy when it calls |
|---|---:|---:|
| Unpaired item-SE rule (1.96 x hypot of item SEs) | 0.75 | 0.886 |
| Fixed 1% relative band | 0.89 | 0.852 |
| Seed-calibrated: seed variance = 2.69 x item variance, fit at 150M only | 0.61 | 0.919 |

The seed-calibrated rule is the item-SE rule with the threshold widened by sqrt(2.69) = 1.64, so it is stricter by construction, and a higher hit rate on its calls is expected. It gets fewer pairs right overall (56% of all pairs vs 67%). The useful part is the 2.69 itself: on a fixed benchmark, a 1.96 item-SE threshold is only 1.2 seed SDs here, so under a normal approximation two equal recipes would be called different about 23% of the time instead of 5%.

### 4. Forecasting seed noise across scale (negative result)

I fit log seed variance as a power law in compute on the smaller sizes, and scored the forecast on held-out larger ones. On DataDecide (the 5-recipe subset, fit on 150M to 530M, 1B held out), it beat the best simple baseline in only 4 of 20 task and metric groups. A simpler rule did better there (seed variance as a fixed multiple of item variance), winning 11 of 20, though only 5 of 20 at 750M.

On the Delphi GSM8K rollouts, both lost to the best baseline at 1e21 and 1e22. Seed noise on the main hinted metric dropped from 2.8 points at 1e21 to 0.26 points at 1e22, while the power law expected it to keep growing. So I don't think a compute-only law is the right way to set thresholds per rung, at least with 3 seeds, and a ratio fit at one scale may not carry to another.

### Smaller things

- Scoring the same 1e21 default weights twice (first pass) gave identical per-question values, so eval nondeterminism isn't behind the seed differences.
- Between pairs of Delphi seeds, 39% to 65% of MMLU answers change, and correctness flips on 24% to 34% of questions.
- On MMLU 0-shot, a question that flips between seeds at 1e21 is only a little more likely to flip at 1e22 (0.49 vs 0.40, phi 0.10). This one is exploratory.
- As a sanity check, refitting Chinchilla Approach 2 on `delphi-blog-data` reproduces Delphi's published optimal model sizes within about 3%. Fit only up to 3e20, it predicts the released losses at 1e21, 1e22 and 1e23 within 0.3%.

## Fidelity against Marin's published default-seed numbers

I averaged every metric per subject, because that is what matches Marin's published numbers. The fork's group value does the same for `choice_logprob`, but weights accuracy by subject size (0.2700 at 1e21 and 0.4110 at 1e22), so its group accuracy won't match the blog at 1e22. Each pair is this run vs `delphi-blog-data`.

| Metric | 1e21 | 1e22 |
|---|---|---|
| MMLU 0-shot accuracy | 0.2703 vs 0.2710 | 0.4191 vs 0.4192 |
| MMLU 0-shot `choice_logprob` | -1.51430 vs -1.51440 | -1.29253 vs -1.29259 |
| MMLU 5-shot accuracy | 0.2783 vs 0.2751 | 0.4675 vs 0.4699 |
| MMLU 5-shot `choice_logprob` | -1.48028 vs -1.47965 | -1.21529 vs -1.21474 |
| GSM8K 5-shot BPB | 0.5637 vs 0.5631 | 0.4391 vs 0.4384 |
| HumanEval 10-shot BPB | 0.6147 vs 0.5195 | 0.4819 vs 0.4136 |

HumanEval doesn't match, and I haven't found why yet. It isn't truncation: the longest context is 2,669 tokens. GSM8K matches with the same BPB formula. If anyone knows how the HumanEval numbers in the Delphi post were produced (backend, tokenization of the solution, few-shot source), I'd love to fix it. Until then I'm treating the HumanEval rows as this harness only.

## Evidence and setup

- Command for the first pass: `lm_eval --model hf --model_args pretrained=<checkpoint>,dtype=bfloat16 --tasks mmlu_sl_verb,logprob_gsm8k_5shot,logprob_humaneval_10shot --include_path <tasks dir> --batch_size auto --log_samples --output_path <out>`. The 5-shot pass used `--tasks mmlu_sl_verb --num_fewshot 5`.
- Versions: lm-eval 0.4.9.1 from the fork, transformers 4.57.6, datasets 3.6.0, on the `runpod/pytorch:1.0.2-cu1281-torch280-ubuntu2404` image with one H100 80GB.
- Delphi revisions:
  - 1e21: `37bd7d2`, `cf238a2` (seed 42), `63f48f1` (seed 62746).
  - 1e22: `8ac3229`, `fb30c1b` (seed 42), `fcc5ce0` (seed 62746).
  - Blog data: `78f8e0c`.
- Cost: 13 runs (6 checkpoints x 2 passes, plus one A/A repeat) in 4.36 billed H100-hours, including installs and downloads.
  - A 3.4B first pass took about 7 minutes of eval time.
  - MMLU 5-shot is 41.9M tokens per checkpoint, and 0-shot is 7.3M.
- Process: I committed the plans for the forecast (Result 4) and the eval selection (Results 2 and 3) before scoring the held-out data. The ratio tables, the target check in Result 2 and the flip analysis are exploratory. I can share the notes, the per-question outputs and the scripts.

## Limits

- Only 3 seeds per configuration, so a single seed SD is uncertain by roughly 0.5x to 6x (95%), and I lean on pooling across recipes and metrics.
- Two families (OLMo-style DataDecide up to 1B, and Delphi). Delphi has no recipe pairs, so the decision-accuracy results come from DataDecide only.
- These are pretraining log-likelihood evals. Loop evals generate answers, and an earlier version of the #10740 description reported 210 of 1,500 task scores changing between two greedy passes of the same weights, so the numbers here may not carry over. The method should.
- The 1e21 W&B configs set trainer seeds 0, 42 and 62746 with `data_seed` null, and Levanter then derives the data order from the trainer seed. So each seed changes both initialization and data order, and I can't say which one drives the noise. The 1e21 default run also used a different code commit (`de20b33`) from the two seed runs (`67099b9`). I haven't checked the 1e22 configs.

## Asks

- **@Calvin-Xu**: to test the eval-selection result on Marin's own mixtures, I'd need the same mixtures run at a small and a larger rung with the same evals. The public `grug-moe-mix-swarm` has 10 seed repeats of a proportional mix at d512, and 10 runs of a proportional mix at d768 (their names show different loader settings too), but the two use different stores, and I couldn't match any d512 design to a d768 one. Do you know if a two-rung set like that exists?
- **@penfever**: would a per-metric seed-noise table be useful for the tie rule in #10197, maybe with a separate threshold for soft metrics? I realize it matters more for recipe calls than for picking a fixed release checkpoint.
- **@Helw150** and **@RohithKuditipudi**: the 20 seed checkpoints from #10555 (blocked by #10758), or just their per-question eval outputs, would let me fit noise for multiple-choice metrics across eleven budgets instead of two. Even 3e19 and 3e20 would help.
- And if anyone is already looking at seed noise on the Delphi ladder, I'd really like to compare notes rather than duplicate it

Thanks for reading, and for putting all of this out in the open

_Edited Nov 21: fixed the accuracy claim (item SE understates seed noise for some accuracy metrics too), described the 5-recipe DataDecide subset, and corrected the rollout counts, the budget count, the MMLU aggregation note, the Result 3 reading and two links. Added #10753, the #5247 context and an exploratory target check in Result 2._

issues.title: Training-seed noise in eval comparisons: measurements on the Delphi seeds and DataDecide

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Follow-up to #11534. #11552 fixed the `--permanent` case of the forced final checkpoint save. Two cases still leave the step that discovery selects unloadable if the process dies while `manifest.json` is open:

- **Default mode:** the last save was temporary and `temporary_base_path` is unset.
- **Restart:** a completed run is restarted. A new `Checkpointer` starts with `_last_save_step = 0`, so the forced hooks in `train()` rewrite the step they just loaded, whether that step was saved as permanent or temporary.

In both cases `step-N/manifest.json` is truncated, and loading fails with `ValidationError: ... Invalid JSON: EOF while parsing a value`.

We tested the fix proposed in #11534 (items 1 and 3 from the issue body) on `main` at `cb991a5`, CPU only, local file system. Both items are needed. Item 1 alone fixes every crash point we tested. Item 3 alone fails the restart cases, because it relies on in-memory `_last_save_*` state that a new `Checkpointer` does not have. Item 3 also removes the whole re-save in the default mode, which closes the untested window where the array data is re-written.

Does the step selected by discovery load after the kill?

| Mode | `main` | Item 1 only | Item 3 only | Items 1 + 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| default (last save temporary, `temporary_base_path` unset) | fail | pass | pass (no re-save) | pass (no re-save) |
| `--permanent` | pass (#11552) | pass | pass | pass |
| `--restart` (last step temporary) | fail | pass | fail | pass |
| `--restart --permanent` | fail; no loadable checkpoint remains | pass | fail | pass |

`uv run --package marin-levanter --group test pytest tests -k checkpoint -x -q` (from `lib/levanter`): 115 passed with both items applied.

## Required changes

1. **Write `manifest.json` atomically on local paths** in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint_manifest.py` `write_manifest`. Do this through `rigging.filesystem.atomic.atomic_rename`, as `_save_metadata` does for `metadata.json`. Remote paths (GCS/S3) keep the plain write: object stores publish an object only when its write completes, and `atomic_rename` on S3 would be a copy plus delete, which protected prefixes deny.
2. **Promote a forced save instead of re-saving** in `Checkpointer.on_step` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py`). This applies when `force` is set, `step` equals `_last_save_step`, and `temporary_base_path` is None:
   - wait for the pending save;
   - rewrite only `metadata.json` with `is_temporary=False` through `_save_metadata(..., extra_metadata=self.metadata)`;
   - on process 0, drop that path from `_temporary_checkpoints` and prune with keep=0;
   - set `_last_save_permanent = True`, and return.

   When `temporary_base_path` is set, keep today's behavior: a fresh `base_path/step-N` write never touches a committed directory.
3. **Initialize `_last_save_step` to `None`**, not `0`. Without this, change 2 makes a forced step-0 save on a new `Checkpointer` look "already saved", and `step-0/` is never written. That breaks `test_train_lm_initialize_model_from_checkpoint`.

Keep the diff limited to these three changes. The tested diff is +21/−1 across two files:

<details><summary>Tested diff against cb991a5</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py b/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py
index 5acffef01f..4db5031864 100644
--- a/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py
+++ b/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py
@@ -527,7 +527,7 @@ class Checkpointer:
         self.keep_params = keep_params
         self._dt_now_injection = dt_now_injection or datetime.datetime.now
         self._last_save_time = self._dt_now_injection()
-        self._last_save_step = 0
+        self._last_save_step: int | None = None
         self._last_save_permanent = False
         self.keep_last_temporary_checkpoints = keep_last_temporary_checkpoints
         self.debug = debug or CheckpointDebugConfig()
@@ -619,6 +619,17 @@ class Checkpointer:
             # The final hook must still surface a failed pending save before later hooks run.
             self._manager.wait_until_finished()
             return
+        if force and step == self._last_save_step and self.temporary_base_path is None:
+            # This step's temporary save already committed step-N/ under base_path. Promote it to permanent
+            # by rewriting only metadata.json instead of re-serializing into the committed directory.
+            self._manager.wait_until_finished()
+            checkpoint_path = os.path.join(self.base_path, f"step-{step}")
+            _save_metadata(checkpoint_path, step, is_temporary=False, extra_metadata=self.metadata)
+            if jax.process_index() == 0:
+                self._temporary_checkpoints = [r for r in self._temporary_checkpoints if r.path != checkpoint_path]
+                self._prune_temporary_checkpoints(0)
+            self._last_save_permanent = True
+            return
 
         my_should_save = force or requested_retention is not None
         my_save_permanent_ckpt = force or requested_retention == CheckpointRetention.PERMANENT
diff --git a/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint_manifest.py b/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint_manifest.py
index 51bb7cd233..39a9d15e37 100644
--- a/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint_manifest.py
+++ b/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint_manifest.py
@@ -13,6 +13,7 @@ from typing import Sequence
 
 from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
 
+from rigging.filesystem.atomic import atomic_rename
 from rigging.filesystem.storage_path import StoragePath, prefix_join
 
 logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
@@ -62,7 +63,15 @@ def manifest_path(checkpoint_root: str) -> str:
 
 
 def write_manifest(checkpoint_root: str, manifest: CheckpointManifest) -> None:
-    StoragePath(manifest_path(checkpoint_root)).write_text(manifest.model_dump_json(indent=2))
+    path = StoragePath(manifest_path(checkpoint_root))
+    data = manifest.model_dump_json(indent=2)
+    if path.is_remote:
+        # Object stores publish an object only when its write completes; see _save_metadata in checkpoint.py.
+        path.write_text(data)
+        return
+    # A forced re-save rewrites manifest.json under an already committed metadata.json.
+    with atomic_rename(str(path)) as temporary_path:
+        StoragePath(temporary_path).write_text(data)
 
 
 def read_manifest(checkpoint_root: str) -> CheckpointManifest | None:
```
</details>

## Reproduction harness

This is a variant of the #11534 script. It kills the process when the forced save opens, for writing, any file in `step-N/` whose name starts with `manifest.json`, so the `atomic_rename` temporary file `manifest.json.tmp.<hex>` counts too. The issue's original script only matches `manifest.json` exactly, so it can no longer fire once the write goes through a temporary file. `--restart` saves cleanly in run 1, then makes the forced save from a fresh `Checkpointer` in run 2, as a restarted completed run does. `--crash-on=metadata.json` tests the metadata window.

<details><summary>resave_harness.py</summary>

```python
"""Variant of the #11534 script.

  python resave_harness.py [--permanent] [--restart] [--crash-on=manifest.json]

Kills the process when the forced re-save opens, for writing, any file in step-N/ whose basename starts
with the --crash-on prefix (so the atomic_rename temporary file manifest.json.tmp.<hex> also counts).
--restart: run 1 saves steps 1..N and exits cleanly; run 2 builds a fresh Checkpointer (as a restarted
completed run does) and makes the forced save; run 3 discovers and loads.
"""
import builtins
import datetime
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time

import jax.numpy as jnp
from levanter.checkpoint import Checkpointer, CheckpointInterval, latest_checkpoint_path, load_checkpoint

STATE = {"model": jnp.arange(4.0)}
LAST = 2 if "--permanent" in sys.argv else 3
RESTART = "--restart" in sys.argv
PREFIX = next((a.split("=", 1)[1] for a in sys.argv if a.startswith("--crash-on=")), "manifest.json")


def checkpointer(base):
    return Checkpointer(base, save_interval=datetime.timedelta(milliseconds=1),
                        step_policies=[CheckpointInterval(every=2)])


def install_crash():
    real_open = builtins.open
    target_dir = f"step-{LAST}"

    def crashing_open(file, mode="r", *args, **kwargs):
        f = real_open(file, mode, *args, **kwargs)
        p = str(file)
        if ("w" in mode or "a" in mode) and os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(p)) == target_dir \
                and os.path.basename(p).startswith(PREFIX):
            print(f"killing at open of {os.path.basename(p)}", flush=True)
            os._exit(137)
        return f

    builtins.open = crashing_open


def save_steps(ckpt):
    for step in range(1, LAST + 1):
        time.sleep(0.01)
        ckpt.on_step(tree=STATE, step=step)
        ckpt.wait_until_finished()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if sys.argv[1:2] == ["save"]:
        save_steps(checkpointer(sys.argv[2]))
        sys.exit(0)
    if sys.argv[1:2] == ["crash"]:
        ckpt = checkpointer(sys.argv[2])
        if not RESTART:
            save_steps(ckpt)
        install_crash()
        ckpt.on_step(tree=STATE, step=LAST, force=True)
        ckpt.wait_until_finished()
        sys.exit("not killed")

    base = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    extra = sys.argv[1:]
    if RESTART:
        rc0 = subprocess.run([sys.executable, __file__, "save", base] + extra).returncode
        print(f"run 1 (clean) exit {rc0}; checkpoints: {sorted(os.listdir(base))}", flush=True)
    rc = subprocess.run([sys.executable, __file__, "crash", base] + extra).returncode
    print(f"forced-save run exit {rc}; checkpoints: {sorted(os.listdir(base))}; step-{LAST}/: "
          f"{sorted(os.listdir(os.path.join(base, f'step-{LAST}')))}", flush=True)
    path = latest_checkpoint_path(base)
    print(f"latest checkpoint: {os.path.basename(path)}", flush=True)
    try:
        load_checkpoint(STATE, path)
        print("loaded")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"load failed: {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:200]}")
```
</details>

Run with `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu uv run --package marin-levanter python resave_harness.py [--permanent] [--restart] [--crash-on=<prefix>]`. With both changes applied, every mode prints `latest checkpoint: step-N` and `loaded`.

## Known limits (not in scope)

- A crash leaves `manifest.json.tmp.<hex>` or `metadata.json.tmp.<hex>` in `step-N/`. Loading ignores it, and only deleting the step removes it. #10969's cleanup removes only `*.__lock` files.
- In the restart case, the array data is still re-written. Only the `manifest.json` window is protected there; a crash while the data is re-written is untested.
- Multi-process runs are untested. Only process 0 writes `manifest.json`. The new branch depends on per-process `_last_save_*` state, which follows the broadcast save decision.

Done when:
- a PR applies the three changes above, with a behavior test for the default and restart cases (a crash during the forced save leaves the selected step loadable);
- `pytest tests -k checkpoint` passes in `lib/levanter`;
- the PR closes this issue and #11534.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`Checkpointer.on_step(force=True)` rewrites a temporary checkpoint in the same `step-N/` directory while its earlier `metadata.json` still marks it committed. A fresh checkpointer on restart also rewrites the loaded step because `_last_save_step` starts at 0; a local `manifest.json` write can then truncate the selected checkpoint before a crash.

**Relevant code**
- [`checkpoint.py#L530`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L530) — initial save state
- [`checkpoint.py#L618-L670`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L618-L670) — forced save path
- [`checkpoint_manifest.py#L64-L65`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint_manifest.py#L64-L65) — manifest write
- [`checkpoint.py#L936-L952`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cb991a5a5c8af4d670d56757eeae3e59edd4a778/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L936-L952) — metadata publication

# Proposed Fix

The final forced hook reaches `on_step()` after a temporary save at the same step, then re-serializes into the directory discovery already selects. Promote that save by waiting for its commit and changing only its metadata; make local manifest replacement atomic for fresh-checkpointer restarts, and initialize `_last_save_step` to `None` so step 0 still saves. I found no open PR for #11959 or #11534; #11620 and #11628 touch OCDBT commits in other files.
